option_text: To adjust for actual productivity
why_wrong: Adjusting the PMB for actual productivity would mask real cost/schedule performance by moving the baseline itself rather than measuring against it — the same baseline-integrity violation as inflating BAC to restore CPI to 1.0.
governing_concept: The Performance Measurement Baseline can be changed only by approved change orders — it cannot be altered to adjust for actual productivity, in anticipation of contemplated (not-yet-approved) changes, or to account for trends.
corrective_rule: The PMB changes on approval, not on anticipation or on observed performance — formal, approved change orders are the only trigger.
exam_trap: Baseline-as-performance-lever trap: raising or lowering BAC/PMB is proposed to normalize a poor CPI instead of addressing the underlying cost-performance problem.

option_text: $3.20 million
why_wrong: This is BAC/CPI = 2.40/0.75 = 3.20 (CPI=EV/AC=0.90/1.20=0.75), which assumes the historical cost inefficiency continues for all remaining work -- but the stem explicitly states the overrun was a one-time, already-corrected procurement issue and remaining work is expected at the ORIGINAL budgeted rate, contradicting that assumption.
governing_concept: An EAC method (or a decision to keep using BAC as the forecast) is only valid when the continuing-performance assumption it embeds actually matches the performance data and scenario given.
corrective_rule: EAC = AC + (BAC-EV) when the stem states remaining work continues at the ORIGINAL budgeted rate (as it explicitly does here, since the overrun was a one-time, already-corrected issue) -- not BAC/CPI (which assumes the historical, now-resolved inefficiency continues) and not BAC unchanged (which assumes zero variance at all).
exam_trap: Stale-assumption trap: an EAC method (or BAC-as-forecast) whose embedded continuing-performance assumption contradicts the CPI/trend data actually stated.
calculation_path_if_applicable: BAC/CPI = 2.40/0.75 = $3.20 million (wrong assumption: historical inefficiency continues).

option_text: $3.90 million
why_wrong: This is BAC + (BAC-EV) = 2.40 + 1.50 = 3.90, substituting BAC for AC as the cost-to-date term in the composite EAC formula -- the correct formula uses AC (actual cost incurred), not BAC (total authorized budget), as its first term.
governing_concept: EAC = AC + (BAC-EV) when remaining work is expected at the original budgeted rate: the first term must be actual cost incurred to date, not total budget.
corrective_rule: The corrective_rule states the correct AC-based formula; substituting BAC for AC (2.40+1.50=3.90) is not a recognized EAC relationship for this assumption.
exam_trap: Wrong-operation trap: EAC/VAC operands that should be subtracted or divided are instead added or multiplied.
calculation_path_if_applicable: BAC + (BAC-EV) = 2.40 + 1.50 = $3.90 million (wrong operand: BAC used in place of AC).

option_identity: Approve the transfer because any unfavorable control-account variance is automatically an unknown-unknown
option_text: Approve the transfer because any unfavorable control-account variance is automatically an unknown-unknown
why_wrong: This mischaracterizes an already-occurred, already-accumulated cost overrun (a known, realized event) as an 'unknown-unknown' (the risk category MR is meant to cover), which is precisely the prohibited use of MR: offsetting a known, accumulated over-run rather than an unforeseen future risk event.
governing_concept: Management Reserve sits outside the Performance Measurement Baseline, has no assigned scope, and prudent-use rules explicitly prohibit using it to offset accumulated cost or schedule over/under-runs that have already occurred in existing control accounts.
corrective_rule: MR may never be used to erase or absorb an already-accumulated, already-occurred control-account variance.
exam_trap: Overrun-absorption trap: Management Reserve is proposed to offset an already-accumulated control-account overrun, contrary to prudent-use rules.

option_identity: Move the overrun to undistributed budget so the original control-account performance is preserved
option_text: Move the overrun to undistributed budget so the original control-account performance is preserved
why_wrong: Relocating the overrun into undistributed budget to preserve the control account's reported performance masks a real, already-occurred cost problem through budget reclassification rather than addressing it -- historical performance should remain visible, not be hidden by moving costs between PMB components.
governing_concept: The Performance Measurement Baseline's component budgets (control accounts, planning packages, undistributed budget) exist to preserve accurate, traceable performance history; moving actual variance between them to improve a reported number, rather than through formal, scope-driven change control, is never a valid basis.
corrective_rule: Historical control-account performance must remain visible and traceable; relocating an already-incurred overrun to a different PMB component to hide it violates that traceability requirement.
exam_trap: Baseline-as-performance-lever trap: budget/baseline structure is manipulated (relocated, reclassified, or altered) to mask a real cost-performance problem instead of addressing it.

option_identity: EV=$280,000; CV=$0; CPI=1.00, because actual cost defines earned progress
option_text: EV=$280,000; CV=$0; CPI=1.00, because actual cost defines earned progress
why_wrong: This sets EV equal to AC ($280,000) directly, treating actual cost incurred as if it defined earned progress -- but EV must reflect completed, weighted milestone value (design+procurement=50% of BAC=$250,000), not spending; AC and EV are different quantities that happen to be compared, not substitutes for each other.
governing_concept: Earned Value is the time-phased value of completed, verified physical work (here, completed weighted milestones), never a restatement of what was spent.
corrective_rule: EV must be computed from completed milestone weights x BAC, never set equal to AC.
exam_trap: Three-way EVM-quantity substitution trap: PV, EV, or AC is substituted for one of the other two in a performance measure or baseline-building step.
calculation_path_if_applicable: AC = $280,000 substituted directly for EV (wrong: EV must come from completed milestone weight x BAC = 0.50 x 500,000 = 250,000).
source_support: S&K6 Ch.14 Earned Value Overview (CCP practice pool challenge item)

option_identity: EV=$350,000; CV=+$70,000; CPI≈1.25, because installation has started
option_text: EV=$350,000; CV=+$70,000; CPI≈1.25, because installation has started
why_wrong: $350,000 (70% of BAC) does not reproduce from any single, defensible weighting error checked: it is not the sum of any two milestone weights (20/30/50 pair sums are 50%, 70%, 80% -- 70% only arises from 20%+50%, which would require BOTH crediting installation's full weight merely for starting AND omitting procurement's already-complete 30%, a compound rather than single error). CV(+70,000) and CPI(1.25) are internally consistent with EV=350,000 and the given AC=280,000, but no single confirmed calculation path was found for the 350,000 figure itself.
governing_concept: Weighted-milestone earned value credits ONLY the weights of milestones that are actually fully complete; design (20%) and procurement (30%) are complete here, so EV = (0.20+0.30) x BAC = 0.50 x 500,000 = 250,000 -- installation (50%) earns nothing until it too is fully complete.
corrective_rule: Sum only the weights of FULLY completed milestones and multiply by BAC; a started-but-unfinished milestone (installation here) contributes zero credit under this technique.
exam_trap: NO_SPECIFIC_TRAP_IDENTIFIED
calculation_path_if_applicable: Checked: 20%+30%=50% (=EV_correct); 20%+50%=70% (requires two simultaneous errors, not one); 30%+50%=80%; no single-step misapplication of the milestone weights lands on 70% exactly.
source_support: S&K6 Ch.14 Earned Value Overview (CCP practice pool challenge item)

option_identity: EV=$500,000; CV=+$220,000; CPI≈1.79, because all scope is authorized
option_text: EV=$500,000; CV=+$220,000; CPI≈1.79, because all scope is authorized
why_wrong: This credits the full BAC ($500,000) as earned because all scope is authorized -- but authorization is not completion; installation (50% of the weight) has not finished, so its value is not yet earned regardless of whether the work package as a whole is authorized to proceed.
governing_concept: Earned value must be grounded in verified physical accomplishment (completed milestones), not in whether scope has been authorized to begin.
corrective_rule: Authorization to perform work is a precondition for earning value, not a substitute for the completion evidence that actually earns it.
exam_trap: EV-independent-of-physical-progress trap: reported EV is accepted despite a material, unreconciled gap from verified physical progress (here: authorized scope mistaken for completed scope).
calculation_path_if_applicable: 100% x $500,000 = $500,000 (wrong: treats authorized-but-incomplete scope as fully earned).
source_support: S&K6 Ch.14 Earned Value Overview (CCP practice pool challenge item)

option_text: Approximately 1.20
why_wrong: This is (BAC-EV)/(BAC-AC) = 6/5 = 1.20 -- the standard TCPI-to-BAC formula, which answers 'what efficiency is needed to recover to the ORIGINAL budget,' not the question actually asked (what efficiency is needed to finish at the APPROVED $12.0M forecast).
governing_concept: The required-efficiency target must use the actual target total (the approved EAC here, not the original BAC) in its denominator: (BAC-EV)/(target-AC).
corrective_rule: Substituting BAC for the approved EAC in the denominator answers a different question (recovery to original budget) than the one posed (efficiency needed to hit the approved forecast).
exam_trap: Wrong-target-efficiency trap: a TCPI-family ratio is computed against the wrong target (e.g., recovery to original BAC, or current historical CPI) instead of the specific required forward efficiency the question asks for.
calculation_path_if_applicable: (BAC-EV)/(BAC-AC) = (10-4)/(10-5) = 6/5 = 1.20 (wrong target: original BAC instead of the approved $12.0M EAC).
source_support: S&K6 Ch.14 Earned Value Overview (CCP practice pool challenge item)

option_text: Approximately 0.80
why_wrong: This is EV/AC = 4.0/5.0 = 0.80, the CURRENT (historical) CPI, substituted for the REQUIRED forward efficiency the question asks for -- it assumes the current rate is automatically the answer instead of computing what efficiency the remaining work must actually achieve to hit the approved forecast.
governing_concept: An EAC method (or a decision to keep using BAC as the forecast) is only valid when the continuing-performance assumption it embeds actually matches the performance data and scenario given.
corrective_rule: The current CPI describes past performance; the required TCPI-style ratio must be computed from the remaining work and remaining approved budget, not read directly off the historical index.
exam_trap: Stale-assumption trap: an EAC method (or BAC-as-forecast) whose embedded continuing-performance assumption contradicts the CPI/trend data actually stated.
calculation_path_if_applicable: EV/AC = 4.0/5.0 = 0.80 (this is the current CPI, not the required forward efficiency).

why_wrong: This assumes parity (breakeven, no adjustment needed) without computing the actual required efficiency from the remaining budgeted work and remaining approved spending -- an unstated, unjustified assumption rather than a derived value.
governing_concept: An EAC method (or a decision to keep using BAC as the forecast) is only valid when the continuing-performance assumption it embeds actually matches the performance data and scenario given.

option_identity: Deterministic, unit-cost takeoff from completed drawings
option_text: Deterministic, unit-cost takeoff from completed drawings
why_wrong: Deterministic unit-cost takeoff is the methodology tied to Class 2/1 (30-100% project definition), where completed/near-complete drawings exist. A Class 5 estimate (0-2% definition) is prepared before such drawings exist, so this method cannot be the correct approach for the scenario described.
governing_concept: Per the AACE Cost Estimate Classification Matrix (Fig.9.1/9.2), estimating methodology is a secondary characteristic driven by the level of project definition: Class 5 = stochastic (factors/judgment); Class 2-1 = primarily/fully deterministic.
corrective_rule: Match the methodology column to the class row in the classification matrix — never assume 'more detailed methodology' is always safer or more correct.
exam_trap: Classic 'more rigor is always better' trap: choosing the most detailed-sounding method regardless of whether the stated scope-definition level actually supports it.
source_support: S&K6 Ch.9 p.91-93, Fig.9.1-9.3 (Estimate Classifications); AACE RP 17R-97/18R-97 (per 10S-90 Cost Estimate Classification System, p.35-36)
notes: Distractor names a real, defined methodology (Class 1/2) but pairs it with the wrong class.

option_identity: Primarily deterministic with some stochastic elements
option_text: Primarily deterministic with some stochastic elements
why_wrong: This phrase is the Fig.9.1 methodology description for Class 2 (30-75% project definition), not Class 5. At 0-2% definition there is no meaningful deterministic component available yet.
governing_concept: Fig.9.1 assigns 'Primarily deterministic' methodology specifically to the Class 2 row; Class 5's methodology cell reads 'Stochastic (factors and/or models) or judgment.'
corrective_rule: Recite the matrix row-by-row from memory only loosely — instead re-derive: lower class number = more definition = more deterministic content.
exam_trap: The option is a real matrix cell text lifted from a neighboring class row, testing whether the candidate actually maps text to the correct class rather than pattern-matching plausible-sounding wording.
source_support: S&K6 Ch.9 p.91-93, Fig.9.1-9.3 (Estimate Classifications); AACE RP 17R-97/18R-97 (per 10S-90 Cost Estimate Classification System, p.35-36)
notes: Directly the Class 2 description per Fig.9.1.

option_text: A vendor-quoted, line-item bid estimate
why_wrong: A firm, line-item vendor bid requires a defined, biddable scope, which corresponds to Class 2/1 (control or bid/tender end usage), not the 0-2% definition level of a Class 5 screening estimate.
governing_concept: Fig.9.1's 'end usage' column ties bid/tender estimates to Class 2 and Class 1, far above the definition level available for a Class 5 feasibility screen.
corrective_rule: Ask what design/procurement information the scenario actually says exists before assuming a bid-based method is available.
exam_trap: NO_SPECIFIC_TRAP_IDENTIFIED
source_support: S&K6 Ch.9 p.91-93, Fig.9.1-9.3 (Estimate Classifications); AACE RP 17R-97/18R-97 (per 10S-90 Cost Estimate Classification System, p.35-36)

option_identity: The identity of the organization preparing it
option_text: The identity of the organization preparing it
why_wrong: RP 17R-97 does not list preparer identity as any of the five classification characteristics (definition, end usage, methodology, accuracy, effort); it is not a driver of class at all.
governing_concept: The level of project definition is the primary, driving characteristic of estimate class; the other four AACE-listed characteristics are secondary and follow from it. Who prepares the estimate (owner vs. contractor) is a separate organizational fact.
corrective_rule: If an option names something not on AACE's five-characteristic list, it cannot be the primary driver.
exam_trap: Exam writers often substitute a plausible-sounding organizational or business fact (preparer, software, dollar value) for the one AACE-defined primary characteristic.
source_support: S&K6 Ch.9 p.91-93, Fig.9.1-9.3 (Estimate Classifications); AACE RP 17R-97/18R-97 (per 10S-90 Cost Estimate Classification System, p.35-36)

option_identity: The dollar value of the project
option_text: The dollar value of the project
why_wrong: Project dollar value is not one of RP 17R-97's five classification characteristics and does not by itself determine an estimate's class; a small project and a large project can both require a Class 5 estimate at 0-2% definition.
governing_concept: The level of project definition (design/scope maturity), not project size or cost, is the primary/driving characteristic per AACE RP 17R-97.
corrective_rule: Class number tracks how much scope/design information exists, not how big or expensive the project is.
exam_trap: Conflating estimate class with project scale is a common real-world and exam misconception.
source_support: S&K6 Ch.9 p.91-93, Fig.9.1-9.3 (Estimate Classifications); AACE RP 17R-97/18R-97 (per 10S-90 Cost Estimate Classification System, p.35-36)

option_text: The estimating software used
why_wrong: The estimating tool/software used to prepare an estimate is not one of RP 17R-97's five classification characteristics and has no defined role in setting class.
governing_concept: Class is set by the maturity of project definition available, independent of which software or calculation tool is used to process that information.
corrective_rule: Software is a preparation tool, not a classification criterion — see also the separate 'Estimating Resources' discussion of software's limited role.
exam_trap: NO_SPECIFIC_TRAP_IDENTIFIED
source_support: S&K6 Ch.9 p.91-93, Fig.9.1-9.3 (Estimate Classifications); AACE RP 17R-97/18R-97 (per 10S-90 Cost Estimate Classification System, p.35-36)

option_identity: Wider accuracy range, higher preparation effort
option_text: Wider accuracy range, higher preparation effort
why_wrong: This option gets the accuracy-range direction backwards: Fig.9.1 shows a Class 1 estimate's expected accuracy index at 1 (narrowest) versus 4-20 for Class 5, so Class 1 is narrower, not wider, even though it correctly identifies that preparation effort is higher.
governing_concept: As class number decreases from 5 toward 1 (more project definition), Fig.9.1 shows expected accuracy range narrowing (smaller index) while preparation effort increases (larger index) — the two secondary characteristics move in opposite numeric directions.
corrective_rule: Narrower class number = narrower (better) accuracy AND higher effort — accuracy and effort are inversely related to class number, not to each other.
exam_trap: A half-right distractor (correct on effort, wrong on accuracy direction) that tests whether the candidate checks both columns of the matrix independently rather than assuming they move together.
source_support: S&K6 Ch.9 p.92-93, Fig.9.1 (accuracy-range/preparation-effort columns by class)

option_identity: Narrower accuracy range, lower preparation effort
option_text: Narrower accuracy range, lower preparation effort
why_wrong: This option gets the preparation-effort direction backwards: Fig.9.1 shows preparation effort index of 10-100 for Class 1 versus 1 for Class 5, so Class 1 requires substantially higher (not lower) effort, even though it correctly identifies the accuracy range as narrower.
governing_concept: Preparation effort increases as class number decreases toward Class 1 because far more project definition must be developed and quantified; accuracy range narrows for the same reason.
corrective_rule: Higher accuracy (narrower range) is 'purchased' with higher effort — the two do not trade off in the same direction as this option implies.
exam_trap: The mirror-image distractor to option A: correct on accuracy, wrong on effort, again testing independent verification of both matrix columns.
source_support: S&K6 Ch.9 p.92-93, Fig.9.1 (accuracy-range/preparation-effort columns by class)

option_identity: Both are essentially the same since class doesn't affect these
option_text: Both are essentially the same since class doesn't affect these
why_wrong: This directly contradicts Fig.9.1, which shows both accuracy range and preparation effort varying substantially and systematically by class (accuracy index 1 vs 4-20; effort index 10-100 vs 1 between Class 1 and Class 5).
governing_concept: Accuracy range and preparation effort are two of the five AACE classification characteristics and are explicitly defined as varying by class, not as class-invariant.
corrective_rule: If a matrix explicitly tabulates a characteristic against class, that characteristic is by definition class-dependent.
exam_trap: NO_SPECIFIC_TRAP_IDENTIFIED
source_support: S&K6 Ch.9 p.92-93, Fig.9.1 (accuracy-range/preparation-effort columns by class)

option_identity: It is required for tax reporting purposes
option_text: It is required for tax reporting purposes
why_wrong: Tax reporting is never identified in the chapter as a purpose of the Basis of Estimate; the BOE's stated purpose is to document design, planning, cost, and risk basis for understanding, review, and validation of the estimate.
governing_concept: The BOE documents scope, assumptions, methodology, pricing sources, and risk basis so the estimate can be understood, reviewed, and traced — a project-controls function, not a tax-compliance function.

The BOE supplements the WBS-organized estimate; it does not substitute for the WBS's structuring role.

option_text: It is primarily useful for early conceptual estimates and adds little value once scope is well defined

option_text: Vendor quotation of every tagged item

option_text: Detailed quantity takeoff with crew build-ups

option_text: USD 10.70 million
why_wrong: This value is close to but not exactly reproducible from the given inputs (12.00 x (250/300)^0.65 = 10.66); it lies in the range produced by small exponent perturbations (e.g., using 0.62-0.63 instead of 0.65) or intermediate rounding of the capacity ratio, none of which is a single, clean, uniquely identifiable substitution error.
governing_concept: Capacity-factor cost scaling is C2 = C1 x (Q2/Q1)^e; the correct exponent (0.65) and unrounded ratio must be carried through the calculation.
corrective_rule: Carry the capacity ratio and exponent through the calculation without intermediate rounding to avoid drifting to a nearby-but-wrong value.
exam_trap: NO_SPECIFIC_TRAP_IDENTIFIED
calculation_path_if_applicable: Attempted reproduction: 12.00*(250/300)^0.65=10.659 (correct); testing e=0.62 gives 10.717, e=0.63 gives 10.698, and rounding the ratio to 0.83 before exponentiating gives 10.631 — several near-miss paths cluster around 10.70 without one exact match.
source_support: S&K6 Ch.9 p.95-98 (Capacity Factor Method, formula $B=$A(CapB/CapA)^e)
notes: Multiple plausible near-miss rounding/exponent perturbations converge near this value; no single clean derivation confirmed.

option_text: USD 10.00 million
why_wrong: This value results from applying the capacity ratio linearly (treating the exponent as 1) instead of raising it to the 0.65 power, i.e. assuming cost scales directly with capacity rather than with economies of scale.
governing_concept: Capacity-factor scaling is explicitly non-linear: cost scales with capacity raised to an exponent typically between 0.5 and 0.85, not one-for-one with capacity.
corrective_rule: If your answer equals a simple pro-rata (linear) scaling of the known cost, you have dropped the exponent — re-check that the ratio was actually raised to the power e.
exam_trap: Classic capacity-factor trap: forgetting that the whole point of the method is the non-linear (economies-of-scale) relationship, and reverting to simple proportion.
calculation_path_if_applicable: 12.00 x (250/300) = 10.00 (linear scaling, exponent omitted/treated as 1.0).
source_support: S&K6 Ch.9 p.95-98 (Capacity Factor Method, formula $B=$A(CapB/CapA)^e)

option_text: USD 9.06 million
why_wrong: This value results from raising the capacity ratio to the reciprocal of the intended exponent (1/0.65 ≈ 1.538) instead of to 0.65 directly — inverting the exponent rather than the ratio.
governing_concept: The exponent e is applied directly to the capacity ratio (Q2/Q1)^e; there is no step in the method that calls for taking a reciprocal power.
corrective_rule: Double-check whether the exponent was applied as given (0.65) or accidentally inverted (1/0.65) during calculation.
exam_trap: NO_SPECIFIC_TRAP_IDENTIFIED
source_support: S&K6 Ch.9 p.95-98 (Capacity Factor Method, formula $B=$A(CapB/CapA)^e)

option_text: Management reserve
why_wrong: Management reserve is a discretionary amount typically held outside the estimate/baseline for management purposes, not a routine, estimator-level placeholder for a known, in-scope element like landscaping that simply lacks detailed pricing.
governing_concept: An allowance covers known, in-scope work whose detailed definition/pricing is not yet available; management reserve is a separate, discretionary fund outside the defined scope basis, per AACE 10S-90's related MANAGEMENT RESERVE concept.
corrective_rule: Ask 'is this scope already identified and part of the defined project?' — if yes but pricing detail is missing, that's an allowance, not management reserve.
exam_trap: A recurring CCP trap: conflating estimator-level allowances (known scope, unpriced) with management-level discretionary reserves (outside the scope baseline).
source_support: S&K6 Ch.9 p.112-114 (Estimate Allowances); S&K6 Ch.9 p.115-118, Fig.9.10-9.12, Table 9.6 (Contingency and Risk Analysis); AACE 10S-90 CONTINGENCY definition p.30

option_text: Contingency for identified risk
why_wrong: Contingency addresses uncertainty/risk in the cost or execution of scope that is already defined and priced; here the landscaping scope is identified but simply not yet detailed/priced at all, which is precisely what an allowance — not contingency — is defined to cover.
governing_concept: Contingency covers variability around an already-quantified value (quantification effort, productivity, wage/material variability); an allowance covers scope that is known but has no detailed pricing basis yet.
corrective_rule: Contingency = uncertainty around a number that exists; allowance = a placeholder because the number doesn't exist yet.
exam_trap: Exam trap distinguishing two AACE-defined cost elements that both 'add money for something not fully known,' but for structurally different reasons.
source_support: S&K6 Ch.9 p.112-114 (Estimate Allowances); S&K6 Ch.9 p.115-118, Fig.9.10-9.12, Table 9.6 (Contingency and Risk Analysis); AACE 10S-90 CONTINGENCY definition p.30

option_text: Escalation
why_wrong: Escalation addresses time/market-driven price increases on cost that has already been estimated; it does not address the absence of pricing/definition for a known scope item, which is what the landscaping placeholder represents.
governing_concept: Escalation is a time-value/inflation adjustment applied to an existing cost basis; an allowance is a placeholder for scope that has not yet been priced at all.
corrective_rule: Escalation changes the price of a known cost over time; an allowance supplies a price where none exists yet.
exam_trap: NO_SPECIFIC_TRAP_IDENTIFIED
source_support: S&K6 Ch.9 p.112-114 (Estimate Allowances)

option_text: SAR 4.00 million
why_wrong: This is simply the unadjusted historical cost with no index adjustment applied at all — the index change from 200 to 300 was ignored entirely.
governing_concept: Index-based cost adjustment requires multiplying the historical cost by (current index / historical index); omitting this step leaves the value unchanged despite a stated index change.
corrective_rule: If your answer exactly equals the historical cost given in the problem, you have not applied the index adjustment at all.
exam_trap: NO_SPECIFIC_TRAP_IDENTIFIED
calculation_path_if_applicable: 4.00 (historical cost carried forward unadjusted).
source_support: S&K6 Ch.9 p.97-98 (index/location normalization within Capacity Factor worked example); AACE RP 28R-03 (Location Factors) and RP 58R-10 (Escalation Estimating), listed in Ch.9 Recommended Reading p.130

option_text: SAR 2.00 million
why_wrong: This value results from correctly computing the 50% index change ((300-200)/200) but then subtracting it from the historical cost instead of adding it — applying the correct magnitude with the wrong sign/direction.
governing_concept: An increase in the cost index (200 to 300) means costs rose, so the adjustment must increase, not decrease, the historical cost.
corrective_rule: A rising index escalates cost upward; if the index went up but your adjusted answer went down, the sign was flipped.
exam_trap: NO_SPECIFIC_TRAP_IDENTIFIED
source_support: S&K6 Ch.9 p.97-98 (index/location normalization within Capacity Factor worked example); AACE RP 28R-03 (Location Factors) and RP 58R-10 (Escalation Estimating), listed in Ch.9 Recommended Reading p.130

option_text: SAR 2.67 million
why_wrong: This value results from inverting the index ratio — using historical index/current index (200/300) instead of current index/historical index (300/200) — which produces a decrease when the index actually rose.
governing_concept: The correct ratio for adjusting a historical cost forward in time is (current/new index) over (historical/old index); inverting it effectively deflates rather than escalates the cost.
corrective_rule: Current index goes on top (numerator), historical/base index goes on the bottom (denominator) — never the reverse — when adjusting an old cost to a new basis.
exam_trap: The single most common index-adjustment exam trap: swapping numerator and denominator of the index ratio.
calculation_path_if_applicable: 4.00 x (200/300) = 2.67 (index ratio inverted).
source_support: S&K6 Ch.9 p.97-98 (index/location normalization within Capacity Factor worked example); AACE RP 28R-03 (Location Factors) and RP 58R-10 (Escalation Estimating), listed in Ch.9 Recommended Reading p.130

option_identity: Remove contingency from the new estimate.
option_text: Remove contingency from the new estimate.
why_wrong: Stripping out contingency is an arbitrary cosmetic adjustment to the total, not a diagnosis of what actually changed between the two estimate versions; it does not identify or address the real scope, quantity, rate, or risk drivers behind the 14% increase.
governing_concept: Estimate reconciliation requires identifying and separating the specific drivers of change (scope, quantities, rates, assumptions, escalation, risk) before any total is accepted or adjusted.
corrective_rule: A change in the bottom-line total must be traced to specific line-item drivers before any action is taken on the total itself.
exam_trap: NO_SPECIFIC_TRAP_IDENTIFIED

option_identity: Use the older estimate because it has already been approved.
option_text: Use the older estimate because it has already been approved.
why_wrong: Preferring the older, already-approved estimate ignores the reconciliation step entirely and substitutes prior approval status for actual investigation of what changed and why — approval status is not evidence that the older number is still correct.
governing_concept: Reconciliation exists precisely because scope, pricing, and risk understanding evolve between estimate versions; the newer estimate may be more accurate, and only driver-level reconciliation can tell which is right.
corrective_rule: 'Already approved' is a procedural fact about the old estimate, not evidence about which estimate is currently more accurate.
exam_trap: A subtle trap for candidates who equate administrative approval status with technical correctness.
source_support: S&K6 Ch.9 p.123-127 (Estimate Review, Basis of Estimate, Estimate Validation, Reconciliation to Past Estimates)

option_text: Apply an across-the-board 14% reduction.
why_wrong: A blanket, uniform percentage reduction assumes the entire 14% variance is a single uniform error rather than the sum of distinct scope, rate, quantity, and risk drivers — it substitutes an arbitrary mathematical fix for actual reconciliation.
governing_concept: Reconciliation requires isolating individual drivers of change rather than applying an undifferentiated across-the-board adjustment to force the total back toward a prior value.
corrective_rule: A flat percentage adjustment to force agreement between two estimates is not reconciliation — it hides rather than explains the difference.
exam_trap: NO_SPECIFIC_TRAP_IDENTIFIED
source_support: S&K6 Ch.9 p.123-127 (Estimate Review, Basis of Estimate, Estimate Validation, Reconciliation to Past Estimates)

why_wrong: This is the direct cost subtotal only (quantity x sum of direct unit costs), with both the overhead and profit markups omitted entirely.
governing_concept: The bid amount requires direct cost, then sequential application of overhead, then profit, each applied to the running subtotal; stopping after direct cost skips both required markup layers.
corrective_rule: Direct cost is the starting point of a bid buildup, not the final bid amount — always check that stated markups were actually applied.
exam_trap: NO_SPECIFIC_TRAP_IDENTIFIED
calculation_path_if_applicable: 1,800 x (75+18+12) = 1,800 x 105 = 189,000 (direct cost only; no markups applied).
source_support: S&K6 Ch.9 p.106-112 (Deterministic/Detailed Estimating, Take-Off, Costing vs Pricing, Unit Rate Construction)

why_wrong: This reflects direct cost with only the 10% overhead markup applied; the second sequential markup (10% profit) required by the question was omitted.
governing_concept: The question specifies both markups be applied sequentially (overhead, then profit) — omitting the second layer leaves the bid understated by the profit markup.
corrective_rule: When a question specifies two sequential markups, verify both layers were applied, not just the first.
exam_trap: NO_SPECIFIC_TRAP_IDENTIFIED
calculation_path_if_applicable: 189,000 x 1.10 = 207,900 (overhead applied; profit markup omitted).
source_support: S&K6 Ch.9 p.106-112 (Deterministic/Detailed Estimating, Take-Off, Costing vs Pricing, Unit Rate Construction)

why_wrong: This applies a single flat 20% markup to the direct cost (10%+10% combined additively as one step) instead of applying the two 10% markups sequentially, each compounding on the prior subtotal — a materially different (lower) result than true sequential compounding.
governing_concept: 'Sequentially' means overhead is applied first to produce a subtotal, and profit is then applied to that already-marked-up subtotal (1.10 x 1.10 = 1.21), which is not the same as a single flat 1.20 multiplier.
corrective_rule: Sequential markups compound (multiply successively); they are not the same as summing the percentages into one flat rate.
exam_trap: A precise, deliberately close numeric trap (226,800 vs correct 228,690) testing whether sequential compounding was actually performed rather than approximated with additive percentages.
calculation_path_if_applicable: 1,800 x 105 x 1.20 = 189,000 x 1.20 = 226,800 (flat 20% instead of sequential 10% then 10%).

option_identity: Exclusions allow assumptions to be omitted because excluded work no longer needs documentation
option_text: Exclusions allow assumptions to be omitted because excluded work no longer needs documentation
why_wrong: This reverses the actual relationship: excluding an item from scope does not remove the need to document it — the BOE is specifically expected to document exclusions (what is NOT included) so readers understand the estimate's boundary, not to reduce documentation burden.
governing_concept: The BOE's design-basis section is defined to document both inclusions and, 'even more importantly,' specific exclusions of items or facilities — exclusions are a documentation requirement, not an exemption from one.
corrective_rule: An exclusion is itself a fact that must be documented, not a reason to skip documentation.

option_text: Exclusions mainly define procurement packaging and are less relevant to estimate reconciliation
why_wrong: This understates exclusions' role: knowing what is excluded is exactly what allows an estimate to be validly reconciled against scope, bids, or later revisions — it is central to, not peripheral to, reconciliation and comparison, not merely a procurement-packaging detail.
governing_concept: Estimate reconciliation explicitly requires understanding scope boundaries (what is and is not included) between estimate versions or against bids; exclusions define that boundary and are therefore directly relevant to reconciliation.
corrective_rule: Exclusions define the comparability boundary of an estimate — they are foundational to, not incidental to, reconciliation.

option_text: Exclusions are recorded mainly to support vendor negotiations after the estimate is approved
why_wrong: This narrows the purpose of documenting exclusions to a single post-approval commercial use, when the actual stated purpose is broader and earlier: enabling readers to understand the estimate boundary for review, comparison with scope/bids, and reconciliation with later revisions.
governing_concept: The BOE's exclusions documentation serves estimate review, validation, and reconciliation throughout the estimate's life, not primarily post-approval vendor negotiation.

option_identity: Present only the most optimistic case as certain
option_text: Present only the most optimistic case as certain
why_wrong: Presenting only the optimistic outcome as if it were certain misrepresents a known material risk as resolved when it is not, which is the opposite of the objective, risk-inclusive documentation professional cost-engineering practice requires.
governing_concept: Estimates are inherently probabilistic; a professional estimator documents the range of outcomes and known risks objectively rather than collapsing them into a single falsely certain optimistic figure under management pressure.
corrective_rule: Suppressing known risk by presenting only the best case as certain is a form of misrepresentation, not diligence or optimism.

option_text: Remove the risk without record
why_wrong: Silently removing a known material risk destroys the traceability and risk-basis documentation that a defensible estimate and its BOE are expected to contain, and directly conceals information management is pressuring the estimator to suppress.
governing_concept: The BOE's risk basis is expected to document how contingency was determined and identify key areas of risk; undocumented removal of a known risk defeats that purpose.
corrective_rule: A risk that is known must be recorded even if a decision is later made about how to handle it — silent removal is not a legitimate handling of risk.
exam_trap: NO_SPECIFIC_TRAP_IDENTIFIED
source_support: General professional cost-engineering ethics principle; consistent with BOE risk-basis documentation requirement, S&K6 Ch.9 p.117-118, 123-124.

option_identity: Alter historical data to support the target
option_text: Alter historical data to support the target
why_wrong: Altering historical data to fit a predetermined target directly falsifies the estimating basis, which is the opposite of the truthful, objective representation of cost information that professional integrity requires, and would corrupt the historical database relied on for future estimates.
governing_concept: Historical cost data underpins conceptual, ratio, and parametric estimating methods throughout the chapter; deliberately corrupting it to hit a target undermines both this estimate and the reliability of future ones.
corrective_rule: Fitting data to a target, rather than fitting conclusions to data, is a core integrity violation, not a legitimate estimating adjustment.
exam_trap: NO_SPECIFIC_TRAP_IDENTIFIED
source_support: General professional cost-engineering ethics principle; consistent with the chapter's emphasis on data integrity for historical-cost-based methods, S&K6 Ch.9 p.94-105, 128-129.

option_identity: Add the same percentage to every bidder
option_text: Add the same percentage to every bidder
why_wrong: A single flat percentage applied uniformly to every bidder does not account for the fact that different vendors may exclude different specific items (freight, taxes, commissioning, spares differ by quote); it fixes an average problem rather than each bidder's actual, documented gaps.
governing_concept: Bid leveling requires normalizing each individual quote to the exact required scope, with each quote's specific exclusions identified and priced, not an arbitrary blanket adjustment applied identically to all bidders.
corrective_rule: Normalize each quote to its own specific stated exclusions — a one-size-fits-all percentage cannot correct bidder-specific scope gaps.

option_text: Discard quotes that contain exclusions
why_wrong: Discarding a quote with exclusions is unnecessary and wasteful when normalization (identifying and pricing the excluded items) is the standard, textbook-consistent way to make an otherwise usable quote comparable — exclusions are routine in vendor quotes, not disqualifying.
governing_concept: The correct response to a quote with exclusions is scope normalization to the required basis, documenting all additions/exclusions, not rejection of the quote.
corrective_rule: An excluded item is something to price and add during normalization, not a reason to reject an otherwise valid quote.
exam_trap: NO_SPECIFIC_TRAP_IDENTIFIED
source_support: S&K6 Ch.9 p.106-112 (Deterministic/Detailed Estimating, Take-Off, Costing vs Pricing, Unit Rate Construction)

option_identity: Use each quoted total without adjustment
option_text: Use each quoted total without adjustment
why_wrong: Using the raw quoted totals as-is compares bids on inconsistent scope bases (since this quote excludes freight, taxes, commissioning, and spares while others may not), making any cost comparison invalid without first normalizing to a common required scope.
governing_concept: Valid bid comparison requires each quote to be normalized to the same required scope before totals are compared; using unadjusted totals defeats that requirement entirely.
corrective_rule: Never compare bid totals directly unless you have first confirmed (or normalized to) an identical scope basis across all bidders.
exam_trap: A classic bid-leveling exam trap: comparing headline totals without checking each bidder's stated exclusions.
source_support: S&K6 Ch.9 p.106-112 (Deterministic/Detailed Estimating, Take-Off, Costing vs Pricing, Unit Rate Construction)

option_text: Only after contract award
why_wrong: Deferring documentation of a material assumption until after contract award defeats the purpose of the assumption register, which is to support review, traceability, and risk management of the estimate before it is used for the funding/award decision it is meant to inform.
governing_concept: Material assumptions affecting price must be documented in the BOE/assumption register at the time they are made so they can be reviewed and reconciled as part of the estimate's own validation, not retroactively after commitments are already made.
corrective_rule: An assumption must be recorded when it is made, not deferred to a point after the decision it informed has already been taken.
exam_trap: NO_SPECIFIC_TRAP_IDENTIFIED
source_support: S&K6 Ch.9 p.123-127 (Estimate Review, Basis of Estimate, Estimate Validation, Reconciliation to Past Estimates)

option_text: Nowhere if management knows it
why_wrong: Informal awareness by management is not a substitute for formal documentation; without a written record in the BOE/assumption register, the assumption cannot be traced, reviewed by others, or reconciled in later estimate revisions.
governing_concept: Formal documentation exists precisely so that assumptions are traceable beyond any one individual's or manager's personal knowledge, supporting review by parties who were not part of the original conversation.
corrective_rule: Personal or verbal awareness is not documentation; traceability requires a written record independent of who currently 'knows' the assumption.

option_identity: Only in the estimator's private notes
option_text: Only in the estimator's private notes
why_wrong: Private, personal notes are not accessible to reviewers, engineering, project management, or later estimators, defeating the traceability and shared-review purpose that formal BOE/assumption-register documentation is meant to serve for a material, price-affecting assumption.
governing_concept: Material assumptions must be captured in the formal, shared BOE/assumption register and carried into risk/reconciliation records — not kept in a location only the original estimator can access.
corrective_rule: If only one person can find the documentation, it isn't serving its traceability purpose.

option_identity: Delete superseded assumptions after each approved revision to avoid confusion
option_text: Delete superseded assumptions after each approved revision to avoid confusion
why_wrong: Deleting superseded assumptions destroys exactly the historical record an audit trail exists to preserve; a reviewer would then be unable to see what changed between versions or why, which is the opposite of preserving traceability.
governing_concept: An audit trail requires dated versions of assumptions to be retained (not deleted) alongside reconciliation logs and approvals, so reviewers can see the full history of what changed.
corrective_rule: 'Superseded' does not mean 'discard' — a proper audit trail keeps prior versions visible, dated, and reconciled, not erased.

option_identity: Overwrite previous estimate files after reconciling each approved revision
option_text: Overwrite previous estimate files after reconciling each approved revision
why_wrong: Overwriting removes the prior version entirely, so there is no way for a later reviewer to independently verify the reconciliation that was performed or trace the estimate's evolution — version control requires retaining, not replacing, each dated version.
governing_concept: Preserving an audit trail requires version control (retained dated versions) plus reconciliation logs and approvals — reconciling and then destroying the 'before' version defeats the purpose of the reconciliation record itself.
corrective_rule: Reconciliation must be provable after the fact, which requires keeping both the 'before' and 'after' versions, not just the reconciled result.

option_text: Use informal manual adjustments when the value is too small for formal revision
why_wrong: Informal, undocumented manual adjustments — regardless of dollar size — bypass the version control, dated-assumption, and approval-record practices the audit trail depends on, creating an untraceable gap in the estimate's history.
governing_concept: An audit trail's integrity does not depend on materiality thresholds chosen ad hoc by the estimator; formal version control and reconciliation logging are the practices described as preserving traceability.
corrective_rule: There is no 'too small to document' exception described for estimate revisions — informal, undocumented changes break the audit trail regardless of size.

option_text: USD 6.34 million
why_wrong: This results from dividing (discounting) the base cost by (1.06)^4 instead of multiplying by it — applying the compound factor in the deflating direction instead of the escalating direction.
governing_concept: Escalation projects a cost forward in time, so the compound factor (1+rate)^n must multiply, not divide, the base/today's-price cost.
corrective_rule: Escalation makes future costs larger than today's cost, not smaller — if your escalated answer is below the starting cost, the operation was inverted.
exam_trap: NO_SPECIFIC_TRAP_IDENTIFIED

why_wrong: This applies the 6% escalation rate for only a single year (8.00 x 1.06) instead of compounding it over the full stated 4-year period.
governing_concept: The scenario specifies 6% compounded annually for 4 years, requiring the (1+rate) factor to be raised to the 4th power, not applied once.
corrective_rule: Always match the exponent in a compounding calculation to the number of periods actually stated in the problem.

option_text: USD 9.92 million
why_wrong: This applies simple (linear) interest — 4 years x 6% = 24% added once to the base — instead of compound escalation, where each year's escalation is applied to the prior year's already-escalated balance.
governing_concept: 'Compounded for 4 years' means each period's growth applies to the previous period's escalated value ((1.06)^4), not a single flat percentage equal to rate times number of years.
corrective_rule: Compound growth over n years is (1+rate)^n, not (1 + rate x n) — the two only coincide for very small rates or short periods, and diverge here.
exam_trap: A very common escalation exam trap: substituting simple interest for compound interest when the problem explicitly says 'compounded.'
calculation_path_if_applicable: 8.00 x (1 + 0.06x4) = 8.00 x 1.24 = 9.92 (simple/linear escalation instead of compound).

option_text: Class 3 corresponds to a nearly complete design and therefore has a fixed definition percentage across industries

option_identity: A universal constant equal to 0.6 for all facility types
option_text: A universal constant equal to 0.6 for all facility types
why_wrong: The text explicitly describes 0.6 as a fallback default used 'if no other information is available' (the 'six tenth's factor'), not a universal constant; the actual exponent typically ranges from 0.5 to 0.85 and is facility/technology specific, and the text further notes the exponent itself changes across capacity ranges for a given facility.
governing_concept: The capacity-factor exponent e is a project- and industry/technology-specific value best derived from an organization's own historical cost-vs-capacity data; 0.6 is only a last-resort default, not a governing constant.
corrective_rule: 0.6 is a 'if nothing else is available' fallback, not the correct value to use whenever better data exists.
exam_trap: A well-known CCP exam trap: treating the historically famous '0.6 (six-tenths) factor' nickname as if it were the mandated or only correct exponent value.
source_support: S&K6 Ch.9 p.95-98 (Capacity Factor Method, formula $B=$A(CapB/CapA)^e)

option_identity: Always equal to 1.0, meaning cost scales linearly with capacity
option_text: Always equal to 1.0, meaning cost scales linearly with capacity
why_wrong: The entire premise of the capacity-factor method is a non-linear cost-capacity relationship (typical exponents of 0.5-0.85, reflecting economies of scale); an exponent of 1.0 would make the method pointless, since a linear relationship needs no exponential factor at all, and the text explicitly frames e=1 as only the theoretical endpoint where economies of scale disappear at very large capacities.
governing_concept: Cost-capacity scaling is defined as non-linear for most facility types (exponent typically 0.5-0.85); a value of 1.0 (linear) is described only as the limiting case at the upper bound of a technology's economies of scale, not the general rule.
corrective_rule: If the exponent equaled 1.0 as a rule, the capacity-factor method would collapse into simple proportional scaling — the method's entire value proposition depends on it usually not being 1.0.
exam_trap: NO_SPECIFIC_TRAP_IDENTIFIED
source_support: S&K6 Ch.9 p.95-98 (Capacity Factor Method, formula $B=$A(CapB/CapA)^e)

option_identity: Irrelevant to the estimate as long as Q1 and Q2 are known
option_text: Irrelevant to the estimate as long as Q1 and Q2 are known
why_wrong: The exponent e is the specific term in the formula that determines how much cost changes as capacity changes; knowing only the two capacity values without the exponent provides no way to compute the cost ratio at all, so the exponent cannot be irrelevant.
governing_concept: The capacity-factor formula $B=$A(CapB/CapA)^e requires all three inputs (A, capacity ratio, and e); the exponent directly and materially changes the computed result, as shown by the chapter's own sensitivity example (a wrong exponent producing ~10-12% error).
corrective_rule: A formula's exponent term is never 'irrelevant' if the formula cannot be evaluated without it.
exam_trap: NO_SPECIFIC_TRAP_IDENTIFIED
source_support: S&K6 Ch.9 p.95-98 (Capacity Factor Method, formula $B=$A(CapB/CapA)^e)

option_identity: Significantly reduces the training time needed for new estimating staff
option_text: Significantly reduces the training time needed for new estimating staff
why_wrong: This is the specific expectation the scenario describes and the text directly rejects: the source states plainly that estimating software 'doesn't convert a non-estimator to be an estimator,' meaning it does not substitute for or significantly shorten the training/experience required of estimating staff.
governing_concept: Estimating software is described as a tool to facilitate preparation of estimates by already-trained estimators, and commercial cost databases still require calibration to specific organizational needs — it augments trained estimators rather than replacing the need for their training.
corrective_rule: A tool that facilitates expert work is not the same as a tool that creates the expertise — software assists estimators, it does not manufacture them.
exam_trap: The core misconception the item is built to test directly — mistaking a productivity tool for a substitute for professional training.
source_support: S&K6 Ch.9 p.128-129 (Estimating Resources)

option_text: Primarily useful for conceptual estimates rather than detailed ones
why_wrong: The text discusses estimating software as a general resource that assists in the preparation of estimates broadly, without limiting its usefulness to conceptual estimates; the passage specifically discussed (p.129) concerns training/experience substitution, not a class-based restriction on software utility.
governing_concept: Estimating software is presented as a general productivity and consistency tool applicable across the estimating process, calibrated to organizational needs, not restricted to any one class of estimate.

governing_concept: Estimating software is described as enhancing accuracy, consistency, and speed for trained estimators, with the caveat that it requires trained users and calibrated databases — not as something to be avoided altogether.
corrective_rule: Correctly rejecting an overstated benefit of a tool does not mean the tool should be discarded entirely — check whether the text recommends avoidance or just tempered, informed use.

governing_concept: Take-off is specifically defined as examining engineering drawings to count and quantify material/labor items, summarized per the project's control structure — a scope-quantification activity, not a price-adjustment activity like escalation.
corrective_rule: Take-off answers 'how much of each item is there'; escalation answers 'how does price change over time' — different questions entirely.

option_identity: A skewed probability distribution and a normal probability distribution, respectively
option_text: A skewed probability distribution and a normal probability distribution, respectively
why_wrong: This reverses which line item matches which distribution shape: the 50/50 under/overrun case (equal probability on both sides of the point value) is the normal distribution (Fig.9.10), and the 40/60 case (unequal probability) is the skewed one (Fig.9.11) — this option swaps the two labels.
governing_concept: A symmetric (50%/50%) probability split around the point estimate defines a normal distribution; an asymmetric split (e.g., 40%/60%) defines a skewed distribution, per Fig.9.10 and 9.11.
corrective_rule: Equal split = normal; unequal split = skewed — match each percentage pair to its shape in the order given in the question, not reversed.
exam_trap: A straightforward order-reversal trap testing careful reading of which situation (first vs. second) was described as 50/50 vs 40/60.
source_support: S&K6 Ch.9 p.115-118, Fig.9.10-9.12, Table 9.6 (Contingency and Risk Analysis); AACE 10S-90 CONTINGENCY definition p.30

option_identity: Both represent normal probability distributions, differing only in scale
option_text: Both represent normal probability distributions, differing only in scale
why_wrong: The two situations have different underlying probability splits (50/50 vs 40/60), which is a difference in distribution shape (symmetric vs. skewed), not merely a difference in scale or magnitude of a shared normal shape.
governing_concept: A distribution is 'normal' specifically because it is symmetric (equal underrun/overrun probability); the 40/60 case is by definition not symmetric and therefore not normal, regardless of scale.
corrective_rule: Symmetry (or its absence) defines distribution shape category; it is not a 'scale' parameter that can vary within one shape while keeping the shape the same.
exam_trap: NO_SPECIFIC_TRAP_IDENTIFIED
source_support: S&K6 Ch.9 p.115-118, Fig.9.10-9.12, Table 9.6 (Contingency and Risk Analysis); AACE 10S-90 CONTINGENCY definition p.30

option_identity: Both represent skewed distributions, differing only in direction
option_text: Both represent skewed distributions, differing only in direction
why_wrong: A 50%/50% underrun/overrun split has no skew at all (it is symmetric by definition), so it cannot be described as a skewed distribution merely 'in a different direction' from the 40/60 case — one of the two cases is not skewed.
governing_concept: Skew requires an unequal probability split; the 50/50 case is the textbook definition of a normal (unskewed) distribution, not a skewed one with zero direction.
corrective_rule: A 50/50 split is the absence of skew, not a skew 'direction' of its own.
exam_trap: NO_SPECIFIC_TRAP_IDENTIFIED

option_text: Variability associated with the quantification effort

corrective_rule: Quantification/estimating variability within a defined scope is exactly what contingency is for — it is the opposite of an excluded item.

option_identity: Labor productivity variability due to weather assumptions
option_text: Labor productivity variability due to weather assumptions
why_wrong: The chapter explicitly lists ordinary weather-driven labor productivity variability among the items contingency IS intended to cover, not among the excluded items — only major unexpected events (not routine weather variation) fall outside contingency's coverage.
governing_concept: 'Items typically covered by contingency' explicitly includes 'weather may vary from that assumed, affecting labor productivity,' distinguishing routine weather variability (covered) from disasters like hurricanes (excluded).
corrective_rule: Ordinary weather variability is covered by contingency; only catastrophic weather events (disasters) are excluded — the distinction is severity/type, not the mere presence of weather.

option_text: Wage rate variability due to inflationary reasons

governing_concept: 'Items typically covered by contingency' explicitly includes wage rate variability from inflationary reasons, changes in crew mix, and market conditions; the excluded-items list instead names 'excessive, unexpected inflation' as a distinct, more extreme category.

corrective_rule: If your answer equals a simple pro-rata (linear) scaling of the known cost, the exponent was dropped — re-check that the ratio was actually raised to the power e.

corrective_rule: Match the EAC formula to the assumption actually named in the question -- 'proceeds at budgeted rate' means Method 1, 'performance continues' means Method 2.
exam_trap: Swapping in the Method 2 (BAC/CPI) answer when Method 1 is explicitly requested is one of the most common EAC-family traps on the exam.
calculation_path_if_applicable: CPI = 80,000/100,000 = 0.80. BAC/CPI = 200,000/0.80 = 250,000 (Method 2, not the Method 1 requested).

why_wrong: $220,000 = AC+(BAC-EV) = $100,000+$120,000, the Method 1 answer (assumes remaining work proceeds at the budgeted rate, CPI=1 going forward); the question specifically asks for Method 2, which assumes the current 0.80 CPI continues -- a different continuing-performance assumption.
governing_concept: Method 2 assumes the CPI observed to-date continues for all remaining work: EAC = BAC/CPI (Eq. 19.7), distinct from Method 1's budget-rate assumption (Eq. 19.6).
corrective_rule: Match the EAC formula to the stated assumption -- 'performance to-date continues' means Method 2 (BAC/CPI), not Method 1 (AC+(BAC-EV)).
exam_trap: Swapping in the Method 1 answer when Method 2 is explicitly requested is one of the most common EAC-family traps on the exam.
calculation_path_if_applicable: AC + (BAC-EV) = 100,000 + (200,000-80,000) = 220,000 (Method 1, not the Method 2 requested).

why_wrong: $160,000 = BAC x CPI ($200,000 x 0.80), multiplying instead of dividing; Method 2's formula specifically calls for BAC divided by CPI, and multiplying produces a value below BAC even though CPI<1.0 signals a cost OVERRUN, which is directionally backwards.
governing_concept: EAC Method 2 = BAC/CPI (Eq. 19.7); division, not multiplication, is the required operation.
corrective_rule: Divide BAC by CPI, never multiply -- multiplying with an unfavorable CPI (<1.0) would nonsensically forecast a cost UNDER the budget.
exam_trap: This operand-correct, operation-wrong distractor produces a number that moves in the wrong direction relative to the known unfavorable CPI, which is a useful sanity check.

why_wrong: $180,000 = AC + EV ($100,000 + $80,000), the same 'earned value substituted for remaining budgeted work' operand error seen in the Method 1 version of this scenario (19-5's $180,000 distractor) -- it does not correspond to Method 2's BAC/CPI formula at all.
governing_concept: EAC Method 2 = BAC/CPI (Eq. 19.7), a ratio, not a sum of AC and EV.
corrective_rule: Method 2 is a division of budget by an index -- never an addition of actual cost and earned value.
exam_trap: This value recurs verbatim from the Method 1 scenario, testing whether candidates recognize it doesn't belong to either legitimate EAC formula for Method 2.
calculation_path_if_applicable: AC + EV = 100,000 + 80,000 = 180,000 (no valid EAC formula produces this figure for Method 2).

option_identity: UCI = 1.08; unit rate performance is favorable (below budget rate)
option_text: UCI = 1.08; unit rate performance is favorable (below budget rate)
why_wrong: 1.08 = Actual $/Credit $ ($6,500/$6,000), the reciprocal of the correctly defined UCI = Credit$/Actual$; with numerator and denominator reversed, both the value and the favorable/unfavorable read are inverted from the true 0.92 (unfavorable).
governing_concept: UCI = Credit$/Actual$ (Eq. 19.9), where Credit$ = Actual Qty x Budget Unit Cost (Eq. 19.8a); credit dollars are always the numerator.
corrective_rule: Always put credit dollars (actual quantity valued at the BUDGET rate) on top: UCI = Credit$/Actual$, never the reverse.
exam_trap: A reciprocal UCI value flips both the number and its favorable/unfavorable label together, so checking only 'does the label match the number's direction' will not catch this trap.

option_identity: UCI = 0.92; the account is behind schedule
option_text: UCI = 0.92; the account is behind schedule
why_wrong: The 0.92 value is the correctly computed UCI, but UCI measures unit-rate (cost) performance in isolation from quantity effects -- it carries no schedule information; schedule status is SPI's job and would require BCWS data not given in this problem.
governing_concept: UCI is the ratio of Credit$ to Actual$ (Eq. 19.9), a unit-rate efficiency measure; it is unrelated to SPI (EV/PV), which is the only index that speaks to schedule position.
corrective_rule: Never read a unit-cost/rate index as a schedule statement -- only SPI (built from PV) addresses schedule.
exam_trap: Pairing a correctly-computed index value with a conclusion from a completely different domain (cost-rate vs. schedule) tests whether the candidate tracks what each index actually measures.
calculation_path_if_applicable: Credit$ = 500 x 12 = 6,000; UCI = 6,000/6,500 = 0.92 (correct value, but schedule conclusion is unsupported).

option_text: UCI = 1.08; quantities exceeded the estimate
why_wrong: This blends two errors: the 1.08 figure is the same numerator/denominator-reversed reciprocal (Actual$/Credit$) as the first distractor, and the interpretation misattributes the result to quantity growth -- but UCI is specifically constructed (using budget unit cost x ACTUAL quantity) to isolate unit-RATE performance from any quantity effect, so it cannot speak to whether quantities exceeded estimate.
governing_concept: UCI = Credit$/Actual$ (Eq. 19.9) isolates unit-rate performance because Credit$ already uses the actual quantity at the budget rate, cancelling out any quantity variance; UCI says nothing about whether the quantity itself grew.
corrective_rule: UCI's whole purpose is to strip out quantity effects -- never use it to conclude anything about quantity growth.
exam_trap: Combining a reciprocal numeric error with a wrong-domain interpretation (rate vs. quantity) is a compound trap that rewards checking both the number and the concept independently.
calculation_path_if_applicable: Reciprocal = Actual$/Credit$ = 6,500/6,000 = 1.083 (vs. correct UCI = 0.92).
notes: Primary code set to INDEX_RATIO_INVERSION since the numeric error is verified and central; UCI_PI_DOMAIN_CONFUSION also applies to the quantity-attribution error and is noted via secondary_error_class=CONCEPT_GAP.

option_identity: Craft wage rates increased after the budget was established
option_text: Craft wage rates increased after the budget was established
why_wrong: A change in the craft wage rate changes the cost PER UNIT of work, not the number of units installed -- this is a unit-rate variance cause, not a quantity variance cause, even though it still produces a cost overrun overall.
governing_concept: S&K6 attributes cost overruns to two distinct causes: quantities installed exceeding budget quantities (inadequate scope, takeoff errors, scope creep, rework) -- a quantity variance -- versus the actual unit rate (dollars or workhours per unit) exceeding the budget unit rate -- a rate variance (p.264).
corrective_rule: Ask 'did MORE UNITS get installed, or did EACH UNIT cost MORE' -- the former is quantity variance, the latter is rate variance; wage/equipment/overtime rate changes are always rate variance.
exam_trap: The exam offers several plausible, real cost-overrun causes and asks which is specifically a QUANTITY variance -- rate-driven causes (wage, equipment, overtime) are a distinct decomposition category even though they also cause an overrun.

option_identity: Always use Method 3 (historical curves) since it's the most sophisticated
option_text: Always use Method 3 (historical curves) since it's the most sophisticated
why_wrong: The text does not rank Method 3 as universally best or 'most sophisticated'; it explicitly recommends using all three methods together to provide a range of possibilities, never favoring one as the single official method.
governing_concept: 'It is recommended that no single forecasting method be used. Rather, include a forecast by each of the above methods in order to provide a range of possibilities' (p.264).
corrective_rule: Never designate one EAC method as the sole official forecast -- always run and report a range from all applicable methods.
exam_trap: Naming a specific method as 'the best, always use this one' is a direct contradiction of the chapter's explicit no-single-method guidance.

option_identity: Use only whichever method gives the most favorable number for reporting
option_text: Use only whichever method gives the most favorable number for reporting
why_wrong: Selectively reporting only the most favorable EAC is precisely the malpractice the guidance warns against; cherry-picking undermines forecasting's purpose, which is to surface real cost risk, not the best-looking number.
governing_concept: 'It is recommended that no single forecasting method be used... to provide a range of possibilities' (p.264) -- the range exists specifically so management sees the full picture, not a selected favorable outlier.
corrective_rule: Report the range from all methods; never select a single number because it looks better.
exam_trap: This option tests recognition of forecasting integrity, not just formula recall -- a classic 'which practice is unethical/improper' item.

option_identity: Skip EAC forecasting until the project is substantially complete
option_text: Skip EAC forecasting until the project is substantially complete
why_wrong: Delaying EAC forecasting until the project is nearly done defeats its early-warning purpose entirely; forecasting is meant to give management the earliest possible view of cost risk, and waiting eliminates the window for corrective action.
governing_concept: EAC forecasting exists so management has 'a range of possibilities' well before completion, when there is still time to act on unfavorable trends (p.264).
corrective_rule: Produce EAC forecasts throughout the project, not only near completion.
exam_trap: This mirrors a broader project-controls principle (early-warning value of forecasting) that recurs across multiple CCP chapters.

why_wrong: 51,200 = (240/1.20) x 8 x 32, taking the correctly computed total labor-hours needed (200, already representing the whole crew's combined effort) and multiplying by crew size a second time -- double-counting the crew.
governing_concept: Total labor-hours needed = Required Qty / Productivity (240/1.20 = 200 labor-hours, already the crew total); Labor Cost = Labor-Hours x Wage Rate.
corrective_rule: Once total labor-hours already reflects the whole crew's output, never multiply by crew size again.
exam_trap: Double-counting crew size after it has already been absorbed into a productivity-based labor-hour total is a very common estimating slip.

why_wrong: 800 = days x hours/day x wage (3.125 x 8 x 32), which omits the crew-size factor from the total-cost formula entirely -- it computes cost as if only a single worker, not the full 8-person crew, were being paid.
governing_concept: Labor Cost = Days x Crew Size x Hours/Day x Wage Rate; all four factors are required to get the crew's TOTAL dollar cost.
corrective_rule: Always include crew size as a multiplier in the total labor-cost formula -- dropping it understates cost by a factor of the crew size.
exam_trap: This is the mirror-image error of double-counting crew size: here the crew factor is dropped instead of doubled, producing a far too small a number.

option_identity: Each new unit requires exactly 80% of the immediately previous unit time.
option_text: Each new unit requires exactly 80% of the immediately previous unit time.
why_wrong: This describes a UNIT learning-curve model (each individual unit takes a fixed percentage of the immediately preceding unit), a different and distinct learning-curve convention from the cumulative-average model the source defines, where the percentage applies to the CUMULATIVE AVERAGE each time cumulative output doubles.
governing_concept: The standard cumulative-average learning curve: average time per unit falls to the learning percentage whenever cumulative quantity doubles -- it is not a flat per-unit-to-previous-unit ratio.
corrective_rule: Confirm which learning-curve convention (cumulative-average vs. unit-curve) a source is using before applying an 80% factor to individual units.
exam_trap: Unit-curve and cumulative-average-curve conventions are both real, legitimate models in the broader literature, making this an easy mix-up even for candidates who understand learning curves generally.
source_support: CCP practice pool (verified); S&K6 Ch.19 Project Labor Cost Control

option_identity: Production capacity must be limited to 80%.
option_text: Production capacity must be limited to 80%.
why_wrong: An 80% learning curve factor describes a rate of improvement in labor time per unit as cumulative output grows -- it has no relationship to capping or limiting production capacity, a completely different operational constraint.
governing_concept: The learning-curve percentage governs how cumulative average labor time per unit declines as cumulative output doubles; it does not constrain how much can be produced.
corrective_rule: A learning-curve percentage describes a LEARNING RATE, never a capacity ceiling.
exam_trap: Unrelated-constraint trap: the learning-curve percentage (a rate of improvement in labor time per unit) is redefined as a cap or limit on production capacity.
source_support: CCP practice pool (verified); S&K6 Ch.19 Project Labor Cost Control

option_identity: Labor cost decreases by 20% every calendar month.
option_text: Labor cost decreases by 20% every calendar month.
why_wrong: The learning curve's percentage reduction is triggered by cumulative OUTPUT doubling, not by the passage of a fixed calendar period; learning curves are a function of cumulative production experience, not elapsed time.
governing_concept: 'Each time cumulative output doubles, the cumulative average labor time per unit becomes 80% of the previous cumulative average' -- the trigger is a doubling of quantity produced, never a calendar interval.
corrective_rule: Learning curves respond to cumulative units produced, not to time elapsed -- a slow month produces less learning than a fast one, all else equal.
exam_trap: Substituting a fixed calendar trigger for the doubling-of-output trigger is a common conceptual shortcut that breaks down whenever production rate varies month to month.
source_support: CCP practice pool (verified); S&K6 Ch.19 Project Labor Cost Control

option_text: 60 percent
why_wrong: 60 percent is the credit assigned to the FIRST step -- pipe placed in its permanent location -- not to the end-connections step asked about; the two steps have different, specifically defined percentages.
governing_concept: Example piping rules of credit: pipe placed in permanent location = 60%; end connections welded/bolted = 20%; pipe trim/ready for hydro-test = 20% (p.263).
corrective_rule: Match each rules-of-credit percentage to its own specific step -- do not swap the placement percentage for the connection percentage.
exam_trap: Rules-of-credit questions frequently swap one step's memorized percentage for another's; always re-read which step is being asked about.
source_support: Ch.19, p.263, Measuring Inputs and Outputs

option_text: 80 percent
why_wrong: 80 percent is the CUMULATIVE credit after TWO steps are complete (60% placement + 20% end connections), not the marginal 20% credited for completing the end-connections step alone -- this conflates a running cumulative total with the credit for the single step in question.
governing_concept: Example piping rules of credit: pipe placed = 60%; end connections welded/bolted = 20%; trim/hydro-test ready = 20% (p.263) -- each step earns its own listed percentage, not a running total.
corrective_rule: Distinguish the percentage credited FOR a step from the cumulative percentage AFTER that step is reached.
exam_trap: Cumulative-total distractors are a common trap in any step-weighted or rules-of-credit question.
source_support: Ch.19, p.263, Measuring Inputs and Outputs

option_text: 100 percent
why_wrong: 100 percent would mean the pipe activity is fully complete (all three steps done: placement, end connections, and trim/hydro-test); completing only the end-connections step earns just its own 20% share, not full credit for the whole activity.
governing_concept: Example piping rules of credit sum to 100% only across all three steps combined: 60% + 20% + 20% = 100% (p.263).
corrective_rule: Full (100%) credit requires ALL listed rules-of-credit steps to be complete, not just the one step named in the question.
exam_trap: Whole-for-part trap: completing one step of a multi-step rules-of-credit activity is credited as if the entire activity (100%) were complete.
source_support: Ch.19, p.263, Measuring Inputs and Outputs

option_text: The bar chart method, and the CPM method

corrective_rule: Keep scheduling techniques (bar chart, CPM, ADM, PDM) separate from labor cost REPORTING systems (earned value, unit rates) -- they answer different questions.

option_text: The Success Index method, and the Productivity Index method

governing_concept: 'The two prevalent construction labor cost control reporting systems are the earned value method and the unit rates method' (p.260); PI is a sub-calculation inside the earned value method, not a system in its own right.

option_text: Only wage rate, with no other productivity factors recognized
why_wrong: Wage rate is not even one of the source's listed productivity factors -- the source explicitly separates the two: 'hourly rates are relatively easy to predict; productivity is the real variable,' and then lists a distinct set of factors (crew size, craft density, interference, scheduling, material/equipment/information availability, rework, site layout, weather, constructability) that affect productivity specifically.
governing_concept: S&K6 lists multiple named factors affecting craft productivity (p.261); wage rate affects labor COST, not productivity, and is explicitly distinguished from it.

option_identity: Because government regulations mandate a minimum of 400 cost accounts on any two-million-dollar project
option_text: Because government regulations mandate a minimum of 400 cost accounts on any two-million-dollar project
why_wrong: No regulation is cited or implied anywhere in the source; 400 is an empirical median observed in a 30-contractor Atlanta study, not a mandated minimum imposed by any government rule.
governing_concept: 'A study of 30 building contractors in Atlanta showed that for a two-million-dollar project, the median number of line items was 400' -- an empirical finding, not a regulatory requirement (p.261).
corrective_rule: A large number of cost accounts is a practical necessity driven by measurement realities, not a regulatory mandate.
exam_trap: Empirical-finding-as-rule trap: an empirical median observed in a specific study is restated as a mandated regulatory minimum.

option_identity: Because labor dollars cannot be measured at all without exactly 400 separate cost accounts
option_text: Because labor dollars cannot be measured at all without exactly 400 separate cost accounts
why_wrong: Labor dollars CAN be measured with far fewer accounts, since inputs (dollars, workhours) already share a common unit of measure; the source's actual point is that OUTPUTS lack a common unit, so many accounts are needed to match inputs to the specific outputs they produced -- not that dollar measurement itself is impossible below 400 accounts.
governing_concept: 'Unlike construction inputs that have the common unit of measurement... the output cannot be measured with a common unit of measure. Consequently, a large number of measures are used' (p.262).
corrective_rule: The many-accounts requirement comes from matching diverse OUTPUTS to inputs, not from any inherent inability to total dollars.
exam_trap: Empirical-finding-as-rule trap: an empirical median observed in a specific study is restated as a mandated regulatory minimum.
