why_wrong: Draft internal figures have not gone through the controls that make the authorized report reliable; substituting them because they are 'more current' trades governance and consistency for a false sense of timeliness.
governing_concept: External requests for the project's financial position must be answered with the authorized, controlled report, not uncontrolled drafts.
corrective_rule: Issue the authorized financial position to external parties, even when a more recent draft figure exists internally.
exam_trap: 'More current' is a common but invalid justification for bypassing the controlled reporting record.
source_support: Current CCP Candidate Handbook (May 2026 Blueprint) 2.F; S&K6 Ch.18; TCM Framework

option_identity: Send the complete project database so the partner can choose which records are relevant.
option_text: Send the complete project database so the partner can choose which records are relevant.
why_wrong: Sending the complete, unfiltered project database offloads the analysis to the external partner and abandons the controlled handling of confidential information the request requires.
governing_concept: External stakeholder requests must be answered with an authorized position and appropriately controlled supporting records, not an unfiltered data dump.
corrective_rule: Provide the authorized financial position with specifically relevant, controlled supporting records under confidentiality terms, not the entire database.
exam_trap: An unfiltered 'send everything' response can look maximally transparent while violating confidentiality control requirements.
source_support: Current CCP Candidate Handbook (May 2026 Blueprint) 2.F; S&K6 Ch.18; TCM Framework

option_identity: Prepare a separate financial position using different cut-off rules from the project’s controlled report.
option_text: Prepare a separate financial position using different cut-off rules from the project’s controlled report.
why_wrong: Preparing an alternate financial position with different cut-off rules creates an inconsistent, uncontrolled basis instead of using the project's single authorized, controlled position.
governing_concept: External requests must be answered from the project's single authorized, controlled financial position with consistent definitions, not a separately prepared alternate version.
corrective_rule: Use the project's authorized, controlled financial position and definitions for every external request rather than preparing an alternate basis.
exam_trap: A separately prepared 'special' version for one requester is a common way controlled reporting integrity is quietly broken.
source_support: Current CCP Candidate Handbook (May 2026 Blueprint) 2.F; S&K6 Ch.18; TCM Framework

option_identity: Export report images as the main historical record instead of structured source data and metadata.
option_text: Export report images as the main historical record instead of structured source data and metadata.
why_wrong: Report images are not queryable, structured records; using them as the main historical record during a migration loses the source data, coding relationships, and metadata needed for future analysis or dispute support.
governing_concept: Systems migration during an active dispute/forecast cycle requires preserving controlled historical data, audit trail, coding relationships, and recoverable source records, not flattened images.
corrective_rule: Preserve structured source data, coding relationships, and audit trail before migration; do not rely on static report images as the historical record.
exam_trap: An image export can look like an adequate 'snapshot' while actually discarding structured, recoverable data.
source_support: Current CCP Candidate Handbook (May 2026 Blueprint) 2.R; TCM Framework; S&K6 Ch.18

option_identity: Retain current summary reports and discard transaction-level history to reduce migration volume.
option_text: Retain current summary reports and discard transaction-level history to reduce migration volume.
why_wrong: Discarding transaction-level history to save migration effort removes the detailed records needed for audit trail and dispute support, which summary reports alone cannot reconstruct.
governing_concept: Systems migration during an active dispute/forecast cycle requires preserving controlled historical data, audit trail, coding relationships, and recoverable source records.
corrective_rule: Preserve transaction-level history and its audit trail through the migration, even if that increases migration volume/effort.
exam_trap: 'Reduce volume' is a common but invalid justification for discarding required historical detail.
source_support: Current CCP Candidate Handbook (May 2026 Blueprint) 2.R; TCM Framework; S&K6 Ch.18

option_identity: Overwrite prior status periods after the new system is accepted by the project team.
option_text: Overwrite prior status periods after the new system is accepted by the project team.
why_wrong: Overwriting prior status periods destroys the historical record needed for the active dispute and forecast cycle, regardless of when project-team acceptance of the new system occurs.
governing_concept: Systems migration during an active dispute/forecast cycle requires preserving controlled historical data, audit trail, coding relationships, and recoverable source records.
corrective_rule: Never overwrite prior status-period data; preserve it as part of the controlled historical record through and after migration.
exam_trap: Acceptance of the new system does not authorize destroying the historical record that must be preserved.
source_support: Current CCP Candidate Handbook (May 2026 Blueprint) 2.R; TCM Framework; S&K6 Ch.18

option_identity: Recode historical periods into the new structure and remove the old coding references.
option_text: Recode historical periods into the new structure and remove the old coding references.
why_wrong: Removing the old coding references after recoding historical periods breaks the ability to trace prior actuals and forecasts back to their original coding, which a controlled crosswalk is specifically meant to prevent.
governing_concept: A WBS/cost-code structure change requires a controlled crosswalk that preserves historical coding so prior data remains traceable, not a one-way recode that discards the old references.
corrective_rule: Maintain a controlled crosswalk between old and new coding structures and preserve the original references rather than deleting them.
exam_trap: Recoding history without keeping the original references looks like modernization but destroys traceability.
source_support: Current CCP Candidate Handbook (May 2026 Blueprint) 2.R; TCM Framework; S&K6 Ch.18

option_identity: Apply the new codes to future transactions and leave prior reports disconnected from the current structure.
option_text: Apply the new codes to future transactions and leave prior reports disconnected from the current structure.
why_wrong: Leaving prior reports disconnected from the new structure, with no crosswalk, prevents prior actuals, forecasts, and performance data from being traced through the structure change.
governing_concept: A WBS/cost-code structure change requires a controlled crosswalk that preserves historical coding so prior data remains traceable across the change.
corrective_rule: Maintain a controlled crosswalk connecting the old and new coding structures so historical data remains traceable.
exam_trap: Applying new codes only going forward, with no bridge to history, is a common incomplete-transition trap.
source_support: Current CCP Candidate Handbook (May 2026 Blueprint) 2.R; TCM Framework; S&K6 Ch.18

option_identity: Combine old accounts into one legacy account so the new structure has fewer reconciliation points.
option_text: Combine old accounts into one legacy account so the new structure has fewer reconciliation points.
why_wrong: Collapsing multiple old accounts into one legacy account for convenience destroys the granularity needed to trace individual prior cost codes through the crosswalk to the new structure.
governing_concept: A WBS/cost-code structure change requires a controlled crosswalk that preserves historical coding granularity, not a convenience-driven aggregation that loses it.
corrective_rule: Preserve the original coding granularity in the crosswalk rather than aggregating old accounts to reduce reconciliation effort.
exam_trap: Simplifying for fewer reconciliation points is a common but invalid trade against required traceability.
source_support: Current CCP Candidate Handbook (May 2026 Blueprint) 2.R; TCM Framework; S&K6 Ch.18

option_identity: Store the final unit rates without the project context so the database remains simple.
option_text: Store the final unit rates without the project context so the database remains simple.
why_wrong: A bare unit rate without project context (scope, basis, date) cannot be correctly interpreted or normalized by future users of the benchmarking database.
governing_concept: Benchmarking data must be preserved with source, units, currency/price basis, scope context, date, and normalization metadata so it can be correctly interpreted later.
corrective_rule: Preserve full context metadata (source, units, currency/basis, scope, date) alongside any stored rate or value.
exam_trap: 'Keep it simple' is a common but invalid justification for stripping out required interpretive metadata.
source_support: Current CCP Candidate Handbook (May 2026 Blueprint) 2.R; TCM Framework; S&K6 Ch.18

option_identity: Convert historical values to current currency and discard the original basis after conversion.
option_text: Convert historical values to current currency and discard the original basis after conversion.
why_wrong: Discarding the original currency/price basis after conversion removes the information future users need to verify, re-derive, or adjust the value under different assumptions.
governing_concept: Benchmarking data must be preserved with source, units, currency/price basis, scope context, date, and normalization metadata, including the original basis behind any conversion.
corrective_rule: Preserve the original basis alongside any converted value so the conversion can be verified or redone later.
exam_trap: A one-way conversion that discards the original basis is a common way traceability is lost during normalization.
source_support: Current CCP Candidate Handbook (May 2026 Blueprint) 2.R; TCM Framework; S&K6 Ch.18

option_identity: Keep the project name and total cost as sufficient metadata for future benchmarking.
option_text: Keep the project name and total cost as sufficient metadata for future benchmarking.
why_wrong: Project name and total cost are only two of the several required metadata elements (source, units, currency/basis, scope context, date, normalization); treating this partial set as 'sufficient' omits what full benchmarking interpretation requires.
governing_concept: Benchmarking data requires a complete metadata set (source, units, currency/price basis, scope context, date, and normalization) for future users to interpret it correctly.
corrective_rule: Capture the complete required metadata set for benchmarking data rather than treating a partial subset as sufficient.
exam_trap: A partial-but-plausible subset presented as 'sufficient' is a classic incomplete-selection trap.
source_support: Current CCP Candidate Handbook (May 2026 Blueprint) 2.R; TCM Framework; S&K6 Ch.18

option_identity: Carry forward last month’s values and update the items specifically requested by management.
option_text: Carry forward last month’s values and update the items specifically requested by management.
why_wrong: Carrying forward stale values except where management happens to ask misses the requirement to reconcile actuals, commitments, forecast, and changes against the current status date every update.
governing_concept: A cost dashboard update must reconcile current actuals, commitments, forecast, and changes to the current status date, not selectively refresh only requested items.
corrective_rule: Reconcile all dashboard elements (actuals, commitments, forecast, changes) to the current status date on every update.
exam_trap: Selective, request-driven updates can look responsive while leaving most of the dashboard on stale data.
source_support: Current CCP Candidate Handbook (May 2026 Blueprint) 3.A; S&K6 Ch.18; Ch.14

option_identity: Use invoice actuals as the dashboard position and add commitments after issue.
option_text: Use invoice actuals as the dashboard position and add commitments after issue.
why_wrong: Issuing the dashboard from invoice actuals alone, with commitments added only afterward, presents an incomplete position that omits a required cost-exposure component at the time of issue.
governing_concept: A cost dashboard update must reconcile actuals, commitments, forecast, and changes together before presenting the position, not issue a partial position and patch it later.
corrective_rule: Reconcile all required cost components (actuals, commitments, forecast, changes) before issuing the dashboard position.
exam_trap: Issuing a partial position and 'adding it later' is a common way to appear timely while actually being incomplete.
source_support: Current CCP Candidate Handbook (May 2026 Blueprint) 3.A; S&K6 Ch.18; Ch.14

option_identity: Report the latest forecast without reconciling it to approved changes and the status cut-off.
option_text: Report the latest forecast without reconciling it to approved changes and the status cut-off.
why_wrong: A forecast reported without reconciling it to approved changes and the status cut-off may not reflect the actual current, approved basis, undermining the dashboard's reliability.
governing_concept: A cost dashboard update must reconcile the forecast to approved changes and the status cut-off before presenting it.
corrective_rule: Reconcile the forecast to approved changes and the current status cut-off before presenting it on the dashboard.
exam_trap: A recent-looking forecast number is not the same as a reconciled one.
source_support: Current CCP Candidate Handbook (May 2026 Blueprint) 3.A; S&K6 Ch.18; Ch.14

option_identity: Use the latest available value from each source because timeliness is more important than cut-off consistency.
option_text: Use the latest available value from each source because timeliness is more important than cut-off consistency.
why_wrong: Prioritizing each source's most recent value over cut-off consistency denies the need to reconcile the differing status dates (Thursday/Friday/Wednesday) before presenting the indicators together.
governing_concept: Cost and performance indicators from different sources must be reconciled to a common cut-off before being presented together.
corrective_rule: Reconcile the reporting cut-offs across sources before presenting cost and performance indicators.
exam_trap: 'Timeliness over consistency' is a plausible-sounding rationale for skipping required reconciliation.
source_support: Current CCP Candidate Handbook (May 2026 Blueprint) 3.A; S&K6 Ch.18; Ch.14

option_identity: Remove the status-date label so differing cut-offs do not distract readers.
option_text: Remove the status-date label so differing cut-offs do not distract readers.
why_wrong: Removing the status-date label hides the known cut-off mismatch from the reader instead of disclosing or reconciling it, making the report appear more consistent than it is.
governing_concept: Any known cut-off mismatch that remains must be disclosed to the reader, not concealed by removing the status-date label.
corrective_rule: Reconcile cut-offs where possible, and disclose the status date and any remaining mismatch rather than removing the label.
exam_trap: Removing a label to avoid 'distraction' is a way of hiding a known data-quality issue.
source_support: Current CCP Candidate Handbook (May 2026 Blueprint) 3.A; S&K6 Ch.18; Ch.14

option_identity: Average the daily positions to create a common weekly status point.
option_text: Average the daily positions to create a common weekly status point.
why_wrong: Averaging positions from different cut-off dates manufactures an artificial status point that corresponds to no real, reconciled date rather than resolving the actual cut-off mismatch.
governing_concept: Differing reporting cut-offs must be reconciled to a real, agreed common cut-off, not blended through averaging.
corrective_rule: Reconcile the reporting cut-offs to one agreed, real status date rather than averaging positions from different dates.
exam_trap: An averaged figure can look like a reasonable compromise while representing no actual verified status.
source_support: Current CCP Candidate Handbook (May 2026 Blueprint) 3.A; S&K6 Ch.18; Ch.14

option_identity: Compare current actuals with the original baseline and omit the authorized baseline revision.
option_text: Compare current actuals with the original baseline and omit the authorized baseline revision.
why_wrong: Comparing to the original, unrevised baseline while omitting the authorized revision makes the approved change appear as unexplained performance variance rather than an authorized baseline movement.
governing_concept: Approved baseline changes must be shown separately from current performance variance so each movement's reason is preserved and approved scope is not mistaken for execution failure.
corrective_rule: Compare current actuals to the current, approved baseline and show any baseline revision separately from performance variance.
exam_trap: Comparing to a stale, pre-revision baseline is a common way an approved change is misreported as a variance.
source_support: Current CCP Candidate Handbook (May 2026 Blueprint) 3.A; S&K6 Ch.18; Ch.14

option_identity: Move the approved change directly into actual cost so the forecast bridge remains unchanged.
option_text: Move the approved change directly into actual cost so the forecast bridge remains unchanged.
why_wrong: An approved baseline change is a budget/baseline movement, not incurred actual cost; folding it into actual cost to keep the forecast bridge 'unchanged' misclassifies the change and distorts both actual cost and the bridge.
governing_concept: An approved baseline change must be shown as a baseline movement, distinct from actual cost and from current performance variance.
corrective_rule: Record an approved baseline change as a baseline movement, keeping it distinct from actual cost and performance variance.
exam_trap: Folding a baseline change into actual cost 'to avoid disrupting' the bridge is a common misclassification trap.
source_support: Current CCP Candidate Handbook (May 2026 Blueprint) 3.A; S&K6 Ch.18; Ch.14

option_identity: Combine the approved change and performance variance into one net movement for simplicity.
option_text: Combine the approved change and performance variance into one net movement for simplicity.
why_wrong: Netting the approved change and the performance variance into one figure hides which portion of the movement is an authorized scope change and which is actual execution performance.
governing_concept: An approved baseline change must be shown separately from current performance variance so the reason for each movement is preserved.
corrective_rule: Report the approved baseline change and the performance variance as two distinct, separately labeled movements.
exam_trap: Netting two distinct movements 'for simplicity' is a common way real performance is obscured.
source_support: Current CCP Candidate Handbook (May 2026 Blueprint) 3.A; S&K6 Ch.18; Ch.14

option_identity: Issue different financial totals to each audience so the report fits their area of responsibility.
option_text: Issue different financial totals to each audience so the report fits their area of responsibility.
why_wrong: Issuing different financial totals to different stakeholders breaks the single-source-of-truth requirement; tailoring should change emphasis and explanation, never the underlying figures.
governing_concept: A single controlled financial position must be maintained, with only emphasis and explanation tailored to each stakeholder's decision needs.
corrective_rule: Keep one controlled financial position and tailor only the emphasis and explanation for each audience, never the underlying totals.
exam_trap: Producing 'audience-fitted' totals is a common way single-source-of-truth reporting integrity is broken.
source_support: Current CCP Candidate Handbook (May 2026 Blueprint) 3.B; S&K6 Ch.18

option_identity: Use the most technical report version for each stakeholder to preserve completeness.
option_text: Use the most technical report version for each stakeholder to preserve completeness.
why_wrong: Giving every stakeholder the most technical version, regardless of role, fails to tailor emphasis and explanation to non-technical stakeholders' actual decision needs.
governing_concept: A single controlled financial position must be maintained, with emphasis and explanation tailored to each stakeholder's decision needs.
corrective_rule: Tailor the explanation and level of technical detail to each stakeholder while keeping the underlying position identical.
exam_trap: 'Maximum detail for everyone' sounds thorough but ignores the tailoring requirement.
source_support: Current CCP Candidate Handbook (May 2026 Blueprint) 3.B; S&K6 Ch.18

option_identity: Report historical actuals and omit forecasts because future values are uncertain.
option_text: Report historical actuals and omit forecasts because future values are uncertain.
why_wrong: Omitting the forecast entirely because it is uncertain denies stakeholders the forward-looking view of financial health that the report is specifically meant to provide.
governing_concept: Financial-health reporting must include forecast and exposure information, appropriately caveated, not omit it due to uncertainty.
corrective_rule: Include the forecast with its confidence/assumption basis rather than omitting it because it involves uncertainty.
exam_trap: Citing 'uncertainty' to justify omitting the forecast is a common way required forward-looking content is dropped.
source_support: Current CCP Candidate Handbook (May 2026 Blueprint) 3.B; S&K6 Ch.18

option_identity: Create a board forecast from rounded management judgment and a separate project forecast from detailed controls.
option_text: Create a board forecast from rounded management judgment and a separate project forecast from detailed controls.
why_wrong: Producing two different forecasts on two different bases (rounded judgment vs. detailed controls) for the board versus the project manager breaks the single controlled position that both views must share.
governing_concept: A single controlled project position must be used for all audiences, summarized differently but never derived from two different bases.
corrective_rule: Use the same controlled project position for all audiences, summarizing for the board while providing driver detail for the project manager.
exam_trap: Two forecasts built on two different bases is a subtle way single-source reporting integrity is broken.
source_support: Current CCP Candidate Handbook (May 2026 Blueprint) 3.B; S&K6 Ch.18

option_identity: Send the full cost ledger to the board and remove summary interpretation to avoid bias.
option_text: Send the full cost ledger to the board and remove summary interpretation to avoid bias.
why_wrong: Sending the full ledger and withholding summary interpretation leaves the board without the synthesized forecast, exposure, and decision content that a portfolio-level financial-health view requires.
governing_concept: A board-level view needs a summarized forecast, exposure, and decision-relevant interpretation, not raw ledger detail presented as neutral.
corrective_rule: Provide the board a summarized, interpreted financial-health view (forecast, exposure, decisions) rather than raw ledger detail.
exam_trap: Removing interpretation 'to avoid bias' is a common way the board is left without the actual decision-relevant content.
source_support: Current CCP Candidate Handbook (May 2026 Blueprint) 3.B; S&K6 Ch.18

option_identity: Report the board position at quarter-end and the project position at month-end without reconciling the different cut-offs.
option_text: Report the board position at quarter-end and the project position at month-end without reconciling the different cut-offs.
why_wrong: Reporting the board and project positions from different, unreconciled cut-off dates leaves two views of the same project that cannot be compared or trusted as consistent.
governing_concept: A single controlled project position should be the basis for both board and project-manager reporting, on a reconciled common cut-off.
corrective_rule: Use the same controlled position and a reconciled cut-off for both the board-level and project-manager-level reports.
exam_trap: Different cut-offs for different audiences of the same project is a common hidden data-consistency issue.
source_support: Current CCP Candidate Handbook (May 2026 Blueprint) 3.B; S&K6 Ch.18

option_identity: Report production quantities without relating them to cost or remaining-work implications.
option_text: Report production quantities without relating them to cost or remaining-work implications.
why_wrong: Reporting raw production quantities without connecting them to cost, contingency, or remaining-work implications fails to answer field leadership's actual question about financial-health impact.
governing_concept: Financial-health reporting to field leadership must connect production/productivity evidence to forecast cost, exposure, and required management actions.
corrective_rule: Connect production and productivity evidence directly to forecast cost, contingency/risk exposure, and required management actions.
exam_trap: Raw quantities can look informative while not actually answering the financial-health question asked.
source_support: Current CCP Candidate Handbook (May 2026 Blueprint) 3.B; S&K6 Ch.18

option_identity: Use the original budget as the main indicator of financial health despite current forecast changes.
option_text: Use the original budget as the main indicator of financial health despite current forecast changes.
why_wrong: Relying on the original budget as the main indicator, despite known current forecast changes, misrepresents financial health by ignoring the most current, material information available.
governing_concept: Financial-health reporting must reflect the current forecast and known changes, not the stale original budget alone.
corrective_rule: Use the current forecast, updated for known changes, as the primary indicator of financial health rather than the original budget.
exam_trap: Anchoring to the original budget despite known changes is a common stale-data trap.
source_support: Current CCP Candidate Handbook (May 2026 Blueprint) 3.B; S&K6 Ch.18

option_identity: Show field leadership the accounting actuals and leave forecast interpretation to finance.
option_text: Show field leadership the accounting actuals and leave forecast interpretation to finance.
why_wrong: Handing field leadership raw actuals and deferring the forecast interpretation to finance withholds the connected analysis field leadership specifically needs to see whether production problems threaten financial health.
governing_concept: Reporting to field leadership must connect production evidence to forecast cost and risk implications directly, not defer that interpretation elsewhere.
corrective_rule: Provide field leadership the connected interpretation (production evidence to forecast/risk implications) directly, rather than deferring it to another function.
exam_trap: Deferring the actual interpretation to 'finance' is a common way the requested analysis is never delivered to the audience that needs it.
source_support: Current CCP Candidate Handbook (May 2026 Blueprint) 3.B; S&K6 Ch.18

option_identity: List the variances without explaining causes so the report remains descriptive.
option_text: List the variances without explaining causes so the report remains descriptive.
why_wrong: A purely descriptive list of variances, without cause, forecast consequence, or required action, fails the variance report's purpose of supporting a decision or corrective action.
governing_concept: A variance report must quantify variances, identify material drivers, explain forecast consequences, and state corrective actions/decisions required.
corrective_rule: Quantify each material variance and explain its drivers, forecast consequences, and required corrective action or decision.
exam_trap: 'Descriptive only' is a common way a report looks complete while omitting the causal explanation required.
source_support: Current CCP Candidate Handbook (May 2026 Blueprint) 3.H; S&K6 Ch.18; Ch.14

option_identity: Remove unfavorable variances from the narrative once a recovery action has been proposed.
option_text: Remove unfavorable variances from the narrative once a recovery action has been proposed.
why_wrong: Removing an unfavorable variance because a recovery action was proposed hides the actual current performance and forecast consequence; a proposed action does not erase the need to report the underlying variance.
governing_concept: A variance report must quantify and explain material variances -- including unfavorable ones -- regardless of proposed recovery actions, until the variance is actually resolved.
corrective_rule: Continue reporting an unfavorable variance and its status until it is actually resolved; do not remove it because a recovery plan exists.
exam_trap: A proposed fix is not the same as a resolved variance and does not justify suppressing the reported figure.
source_support: Current CCP Candidate Handbook (May 2026 Blueprint) 3.H; S&K6 Ch.18; Ch.14

option_identity: Compare actuals with the prior month and omit the approved baseline comparison.
option_text: Compare actuals with the prior month and omit the approved baseline comparison.
why_wrong: Comparing only to the prior month, without the approved baseline comparison, does not measure the cost and schedule departure from the baseline that the report is specifically meant to show.
governing_concept: Variance reporting requires comparison to the approved baseline, not only month-over-month comparison, to correctly quantify the departure.
corrective_rule: Compare current actuals to the approved baseline, using period-over-period comparison as supplementary trend information only.
exam_trap: A prior-month comparison can look like valid trend analysis while substituting for the required baseline comparison.
source_support: Current CCP Candidate Handbook (May 2026 Blueprint) 3.H; S&K6 Ch.18; Ch.14

option_identity: Report the net cost variance without identifying whether quantity or rate caused it.
option_text: Report the net cost variance without identifying whether quantity or rate caused it.
why_wrong: Reporting only the net variance treats it as self-explanatory instead of decomposing it into the quantity and rate components the scenario specifically describes as moving in opposite directions.
governing_concept: Cost variance from a mixed quantity/rate cause must be decomposed into its quantity and rate contributions, not reported as one net figure.
corrective_rule: Separate and explain the quantity and rate contributions to a variance before drawing conclusions or updating the forecast.
exam_trap: A single net number can hide two offsetting drivers moving in opposite directions.
source_support: Current CCP Candidate Handbook (May 2026 Blueprint) 3.H; S&K6 Ch.18; Ch.14

option_identity: Attribute the overrun to the unit rate because cost variance is measured in currency.
option_text: Attribute the overrun to the unit rate because cost variance is measured in currency.
why_wrong: Attributing the overrun to rate based only on the fact that cost is measured in currency ignores the scenario's actual components, where the rate is slightly favorable and the higher installed quantity is the actual driver of the overrun.
governing_concept: Cost variance drivers must be identified by decomposing the actual quantity and rate components, not inferred from the unit of measurement alone.
corrective_rule: Identify the actual driver (quantity or rate) by decomposing the variance into its components rather than assuming based on the reporting unit.
exam_trap: A superficially logical-sounding rationale (currency implies rate) is a common way the real driver is misattributed.
source_support: Current CCP Candidate Handbook (May 2026 Blueprint) 3.H; S&K6 Ch.18; Ch.14

option_identity: Use the favorable rate variance to offset the quantity issue and close the variance item.
option_text: Use the favorable rate variance to offset the quantity issue and close the variance item.
why_wrong: Netting the favorable rate against the unfavorable quantity to close the item hides the underlying quantity overrun instead of explaining each driver and updating the forecast implication.
governing_concept: Distinct variance drivers (quantity, rate) must be explained separately, even when one partially offsets the other, and must inform the forecast rather than being netted away.
corrective_rule: Explain each variance driver separately and reflect the quantity issue in the forecast, rather than netting it against an unrelated favorable driver to close the item.
exam_trap: Netting offsetting drivers to 'close' an issue is a common way a real underlying problem (quantity overrun) is concealed.
source_support: Current CCP Candidate Handbook (May 2026 Blueprint) 3.H; S&K6 Ch.18; Ch.14

option_identity: Remove the approved change from historical reporting so prior baseline history is no longer shown.
option_text: Remove the approved change from historical reporting so prior baseline history is no longer shown.
why_wrong: Removing the approved change from historical reporting erases the record of how and why the baseline moved, destroying the traceability that authorized-change history must preserve.
governing_concept: Variance reporting must distinguish authorized baseline change from current performance variance while preserving the historical record of both.
corrective_rule: Preserve the historical record of an approved baseline change; distinguish it from performance variance rather than deleting it from history.
exam_trap: Deleting an inconvenient piece of baseline history is a governance issue, not a valid simplification.
source_support: Current CCP Candidate Handbook (May 2026 Blueprint) 3.H; S&K6 Ch.18; Ch.14

option_identity: Transfer the approved change value into actual cost and leave baseline history unchanged.
option_text: Transfer the approved change value into actual cost and leave baseline history unchanged.
why_wrong: An approved baseline change is a budget movement, not incurred actual cost; moving its value into actual cost while leaving baseline history unchanged misclassifies the change and misstates both actual cost and the baseline record.
governing_concept: An approved baseline change must be shown as a distinct baseline movement, separate from actual cost and from performance variance.
corrective_rule: Record an approved baseline change as a baseline movement in the baseline history, keeping it distinct from actual cost.
exam_trap: Reclassifying a baseline change as actual cost is a common way its true nature is obscured.
source_support: Current CCP Candidate Handbook (May 2026 Blueprint) 3.H; S&K6 Ch.18; Ch.14

option_identity: Continue comparing with the original baseline and label the full difference as performance variance.
option_text: Continue comparing with the original baseline and label the full difference as performance variance.
why_wrong: Comparing to the original, unrevised baseline and labeling the entire difference as performance variance presents most of an approved scope change as if it were execution failure.
governing_concept: Approved baseline changes must be distinguished from current performance variance so the report does not present authorized scope as execution failure.
corrective_rule: Compare to the current, revised baseline and label only the true execution-driven portion as performance variance.
exam_trap: Labeling an authorized scope change as 'performance variance' is a common and serious misclassification.

option_identity: Communication channels increase only in direct proportion to team size
option_text: Communication channels increase only in direct proportion to team size
why_wrong: The number of potential communication channels in a fully connected team grows combinatorially (pairwise) as team size increases, not in direct (linear) proportion to the number of members.
governing_concept: Potential communication channels among a group grow combinatorially with team size, which is why communication structure becomes increasingly important as teams grow.
corrective_rule: Recognize that potential communication paths scale combinatorially, not linearly, with team size, and plan communication structure accordingly.

governing_concept: Controlling an operating budget overrun requires comparing actual and committed operating costs to the approved budget, analyzing the drivers of the variance, forecasting the year-end outcome, and implementing only authorized control actions -- the CCP Blueprint 1.M responsibility.

governing_concept: Cost/price risk allocation is fixed by the named contract type's payment mechanism: fixed-price/lump-sum and unit-price contracts pay a pre-agreed price for defined scope, so the contractor bears the risk of an inaccurate bid or productivity shortfall (scope unchanged), while cost-reimbursable structures (CPFF, CPIF, cost-plus-percentage-of-cost) and open-ended T&M reimburse actual cost, so cost-growth risk sits mainly with the owner.

option_text: Mark-up costs

governing_concept: Comparing or ranking competing bids requires first normalizing them onto a common scope, exclusions, and commercial basis (confirming each reflects the same addenda, inclusions, and assumptions); raw submitted totals from bids built on different bases -- or an average of them -- are not directly comparable.
corrective_rule: Before comparing or ranking bids, confirm each reflects the same scope, exclusions, and addenda; resolve any gaps through bidder clarification rather than averaging raw totals, borrowing one bidder's basis for another, or ranking before the basis is verified.
exam_trap: Averaging two numbers feels like a neutral, defensible way to pick a single forecast figure, which obscures that the two offers differ in ways (delivery, currency exposure) that an average simply erases rather than evaluates.

option_text: The owner

governing_concept: Cost/price risk allocation is fixed by the named contract type's payment mechanism: fixed-price/lump-sum and unit-price contracts pay a pre-agreed price for defined scope, so the contractor bears the risk of an inaccurate bid or productivity shortfall (scope unchanged), while cost-reimbursable structures (CPFF, CPIF, cost-plus-percentage-of-cost) and open-ended T&M reimburse actual cost, so cost-growth risk sits mainly with the owner.
corrective_rule: Before answering a 'who bears the risk' question, classify the named contract type as fixed-price/unit-price (contractor risk on defined scope) or cost-reimbursable/T&M (owner risk), then match that classification -- not the option's surface plausibility -- to the party named in the option.
exam_trap: Because the owner pays the fixed price and could be seen as 'committed' to it, a test-taker can mistakenly attribute the resulting price/time risk to the owner rather than to the contractor who must perform at that fixed price.

option_identity: Allow subcontractors and vendors to adjust their prices after contract award
option_text: Allow subcontractors and vendors to adjust their prices after contract award
why_wrong: The official solution states an EPA clause entitles the CONTRACTOR to seek a price adjustment for named items in ITS contract with the owner; it does not grant subcontractors and vendors a right to adjust their own prices after contract award as a chapter-defined mechanism.
governing_concept: An Economic Price Adjustment (EPA) clause is a fixed-price-contract mechanism entitling the contractor to seek a price adjustment for specifically named items in the contract when their cost moves more than a stipulated percentage -- it is not a general repricing right, not held by subcontractors/vendors directly against the owner, and not a right the owner or a construction manager can invoke to change the pricing mechanism at will.
corrective_rule: Confirm an EPA-clause option states the contractor's right to reprice a specifically named item once its cost crosses a stipulated percentage threshold, and reject options that change the holder of the right, its scope, or its trigger.
exam_trap: Subcontractors and vendors are the parties whose costs actually drive the priced items, making it easy to misattribute the contractor's EPA right to them instead.

option_identity: When a contractor is projecting late completion and decides to accelerate their work rather than pay the late completion damages under the contract

governing_concept: Constructive acceleration is caused by an owner/employer action or failure to act (such as wrongly denying a justified time extension) that inadvertently compels the contractor to complete work earlier than required (or should have been required) and causes a cost impact; voluntary contractor-initiated acceleration to avoid the contractor's own liquidated-damages exposure, a contractor's own work-around decision, or an owner granting a time extension without paying delay damages, does not meet this owner-causation, compelled-early-completion requirement.
corrective_rule: Confirm the option describes an OWNER action or failure to act that compels the contractor to complete earlier than required at added cost, and reject options where the contractor initiates acceleration voluntarily or the owner actually grants relief (a time extension).

why_wrong: Reverses the subtraction order in the cash flow formula (Payments − Receipts instead of Receipts − Payments), which preserves the correct $230,000 magnitude but flips the sign to negative.
governing_concept: Cash Flow = Cash Receipts − Cash Payments (Eq.28.1); the subtraction must be taken in that specific order.
corrective_rule: Always subtract Payments FROM Receipts (Receipts − Payments), never the reverse; a positive result means receipts exceeded payments for the period.
exam_trap: A test-taker who correctly identifies the two figures but subtracts them in the wrong order gets the right dollar magnitude with the wrong sign, and may not notice the sign flip if not checking whether receipts or payments were larger.
calculation_path_if_applicable: Reversed subtraction: Payments − Receipts = $620,000 − $850,000 = −$230,000 (verified: 620,000−850,000=−230,000).

why_wrong: $620,000 is simply the cash-payments figure given in the problem, restated unchanged as the answer; no subtraction was performed at all.
governing_concept: Cash Flow = Cash Receipts − Cash Payments (Eq.28.1); the answer must be the computed difference, not either input figure alone.
corrective_rule: Never report a single given input value as the final answer to a two-input formula question; always perform the required subtraction.
exam_trap: A test-taker skimming the numbers may grab the payments figure directly because it 'looks like' a plausible cash-flow number, without realizing the question asks for the net of both figures.
calculation_path_if_applicable: Distractor equals the payments input unchanged: $620,000 (no computation performed).

why_wrong: Adds cash receipts and cash payments together instead of subtracting, producing a figure that overstates net cash flow by double-counting the payments amount.
governing_concept: Cash Flow = Cash Receipts − Cash Payments (Eq.28.1); receipts and payments are combined by subtraction, not addition.
corrective_rule: Only subtract payments from receipts when computing net cash flow; adding the two figures has no valid interpretation under this formula.
exam_trap: A test-taker who treats 'combine these two cash figures' as an instruction to add rather than net them out will produce a much larger, superficially 'busier-looking' number that can feel more thorough.

option_identity: Making a profit is always the same as having liquidity — they can't diverge

exam_trap: A test-taker may assume 'profitable' automatically means 'financially healthy' and pick the option that equates the two, missing the whole point of why cash flow analysis is performed alongside profit reporting.

option_text: PI = 0.83; should not be considered

option_text: PI = 200,000; should be considered
why_wrong: Subtracts the initial investment from the PV of future cash flows ($1,200,000 − $1,000,000 = $200,000), which computes Net Present Value, not the Profitability Index; PI requires division, not subtraction.
governing_concept: Profitability Index (a ratio, PV/Investment) and Net Present Value (a dollar difference, PV−Investment) are two distinct economic indicators built from the same two inputs by two different operations.
corrective_rule: Use division (PV / Investment) to compute PI; use subtraction (PV − Investment) to compute NPV; never substitute one operation for the other.
exam_trap: A test-taker who is more comfortable with NPV's subtraction than PI's division may default to subtracting the two figures even when the question specifically asks for PI.

option_text: Company B is better: 7.5% vs. 12%
why_wrong: Computes both companies' ROCE correctly (A=12%, B=7.5%) but then declares Company B — the one with the LOWER ROCE — as 'better,' inverting the direction of the comparison; a higher ROCE means more efficient use of capital.
governing_concept: ROCE = Operating Income / Assets Employed; a HIGHER ROCE indicates a company is generating more profit per dollar of capital employed, i.e., more efficient capital use.
corrective_rule: After computing both ROCE values correctly, always select the company with the numerically HIGHER percentage as the better performer.
exam_trap: A test-taker may correctly calculate both percentages but then instinctively favor the company with the larger absolute asset base (Company B), mistakenly treating 'more assets' as inherently 'better' and picking the lower ROCE company.
calculation_path_if_applicable: ROCE(A) = 60/500 = 0.12 = 12%; ROCE(B) = 60/800 = 0.075 = 7.5% (both verified correct), but the winner label is swapped: B (7.5%) is called better than A (12%).

option_text: Both are identical at 12% each
why_wrong: Assumes both companies must have identical ROCE simply because they earn the same $60 million operating income, ignoring that their asset bases ($500M vs. $800M) differ, which necessarily makes the two ratios different (12% vs. 7.5%).
governing_concept: ROCE = Operating Income / Assets Employed; equal numerators (profit) do NOT produce equal ratios when the denominators (assets employed) differ.
corrective_rule: Always divide each company's own profit by its own assets employed; never assume equal profit implies equal ROCE without checking the denominator.
exam_trap: A test-taker who fixates on the identical $60 million profit figure may conclude the companies are 'the same' without noticing the problem explicitly gives two different asset-employed figures that must each be divided in.
calculation_path_if_applicable: Falsely assumes ROCE(A) = ROCE(B) = 12% based on equal profit alone, without dividing by each company's own $500M/$800M asset base (correct values are 12% and 7.5%, not equal).

option_text: Company A is better: 7.5% vs. 12%
why_wrong: Correctly identifies Company A as the better performer but swaps the two companies' computed ROCE values (assigning B's 7.5% to A and A's 12% to B), so the winner label is right but the supporting figures are transposed between the two parallel scenario branches.
governing_concept: ROCE = Operating Income / Assets Employed, computed independently for each company; each company's own percentage must stay attached to that company.
corrective_rule: After computing each company's ROCE separately, double-check that each percentage is reported next to the correct company label before finalizing the answer.
exam_trap: A test-taker doing both calculations quickly may correctly determine which company 'wins' from memory of the relative sizes, but then transpose the two percentage figures when writing up the final comparison.
calculation_path_if_applicable: Correct values are ROCE(A)=60/500=12%, ROCE(B)=60/800=7.5%; this option swaps them to A=7.5%, B=12%, an entity/value cross-contamination.

corrective_rule: Memorize the three named ROCE elements exactly; do not substitute a single unrelated balance-sheet figure like cash on hand for the full list.

governing_concept: S&K6 identifies total company cash flow as having three basic components: Operations, Financing, and Investments (Eq.28.2-28.4).
corrective_rule: Memorize the three named cash flow components (Operations, Financing, Investments) specifically; do not import a cost-estimating taxonomy from a different chapter.

option_text: Alternative B
why_wrong: Selects Alternative B as having the lower life-cycle cost, but the undiscounted 8-year totals are Alternative A = $12.00 million and Alternative B = $12.40 million; A is actually lower, so this option selects the inferior alternative.
governing_concept: Undiscounted life-cycle cost (LCC) = CAPEX + (annual OPEX x number of years); the alternative with the lower total LCC is preferred when discounting and salvage are ignored.
corrective_rule: Compute the full LCC for each alternative (CAPEX + OPEX x years) before selecting; never assume the higher-CAPEX alternative loses just because it has lower annual OPEX without checking the total.
exam_trap: A test-taker may notice Alternative B has the lower annual OPEX ($425,000 vs. $500,000) and jump to the conclusion that B must have the lower life-cycle cost, without adding in B's higher CAPEX.
source_support: CCP practice pool (verified) — Life-cycle cost; S&K6 Ch.28 Practical Corporate Investment Decision-Making Guide

option_text: Insufficient information
why_wrong: Claims insufficient information exists to compare the alternatives, but the problem supplies every figure needed (CAPEX and annual OPEX for both alternatives, plus the 8-year period), making the comparison fully computable.
governing_concept: Undiscounted life-cycle cost (LCC) = CAPEX + (annual OPEX x number of years); all inputs needed for this comparison are given in the problem.
corrective_rule: Before choosing an 'insufficient information' option, confirm that all inputs the formula actually requires are genuinely missing; here, none are.
exam_trap: A test-taker intimidated by a multi-step comparison problem may default to an 'insufficient information' escape-hatch option rather than working through the two straightforward LCC sums.

option_text: Both are equal
why_wrong: Declares the two alternatives equal, but their undiscounted 8-year life-cycle costs are $12.00 million (A) and $12.40 million (B) — a real $0.40 million difference, not a tie.
governing_concept: Undiscounted life-cycle cost (LCC) = CAPEX + (annual OPEX x number of years); two alternatives with different CAPEX and OPEX inputs will generally produce different LCC totals.
corrective_rule: Never assume two alternatives are 'equal' without actually summing each one's CAPEX and OPEX; only declare equality when the computed totals genuinely match.
exam_trap: A test-taker who notices the two alternatives are 'close' in cost structure (only a $1.00M CAPEX difference and a $75,000 annual OPEX difference) may round the comparison down to 'basically the same' without doing the arithmetic.
calculation_path_if_applicable: LCC(A) = $12.00M; LCC(B) = $12.40M (verified as above) — not equal.
source_support: CCP practice pool (verified) — Life-cycle cost; S&K6 Ch.28 Practical Corporate Investment Decision-Making Guide

option_text: 0.28 years
why_wrong: Inverts the payback formula (annual savings / initial investment instead of initial investment / annual savings), producing the mathematical reciprocal of the correct payback period.
governing_concept: Simple payback period = Initial Investment / Annual Net Savings; the investment amount belongs in the numerator, the annual savings in the denominator.
corrective_rule: Always divide the initial investment by the annual savings, never the reverse, when computing simple payback period.
exam_trap: A test-taker unsure which figure is the numerator may divide the smaller annual figure by the larger investment figure instead of the reverse, producing a plausible-looking small decimal.
calculation_path_if_applicable: Inverted ratio: Annual Net Savings / Initial Investment = $250,000 / $900,000 = 0.2778 ≈ 0.28 years (verified: 250,000/900,000=0.27778).
source_support: CCP practice pool (verified) — Payback period; S&K6 Ch.28 Practical Corporate Investment Decision-Making Guide

option_text: 0.30 years
why_wrong: 0.30 years does not correspond to any single clean, reproducible operation on the given $900,000 investment and $250,000 annual savings figures (it is close to, but not exactly, the inverted-ratio result of 0.28 years); it is confirmed wrong because it does not equal Investment/Savings = 3.60 years, but the precise arithmetic slip that produces it cannot be pinned down with confidence from the source material given.
governing_concept: Simple payback period = Initial Investment / Annual Net Savings = $900,000 / $250,000 = 3.60 years.
corrective_rule: Always divide the initial investment by the annual savings figure exactly as given; do not round or approximate intermediate figures before dividing.
exam_trap: A test-taker who is already leaning toward an inverted, sub-one-year answer (mistaking savings/investment for the payback ratio) may land on a nearby rounded value like 0.30 rather than the more precisely inverted 0.28.
source_support: CCP practice pool (verified) — Payback period; S&K6 Ch.28 Practical Corporate Investment Decision-Making Guide
notes: Could not derive a single clean, independently reproducible calculation path for this exact value; treated as GENERAL_WRONG_REASON_VERIFIED per the source's own generic whyWrong text rather than inventing an unverified specific mechanism.

option_text: 4.60 years
why_wrong: Adds one extra year to the correctly computed 3.60-year payback period, as if an additional period needed to be counted beyond the point where the investment is actually recovered.
governing_concept: Simple payback period = Initial Investment / Annual Net Savings = $900,000 / $250,000 = 3.60 years; no additional period should be added once the ratio is computed.
corrective_rule: Report the Investment/Savings ratio itself as the payback period; do not add an extra year for 'the year payback occurs' or any other period-counting adjustment.
exam_trap: A test-taker used to inclusive day/period-counting conventions elsewhere in project controls (e.g., adding 1 for an inclusive count) may mistakenly apply a similar +1 adjustment here, where none is called for.
calculation_path_if_applicable: Correct payback (3.60 years) + 1 extra year = 4.60 years (verified: 900,000/250,000=3.60; 3.60+1.00=4.60).
source_support: CCP practice pool (verified) — Payback period; S&K6 Ch.28 Practical Corporate Investment Decision-Making Guide

option_identity: Accepted, because 9% is a positive return

why_wrong: Treats any positive IRR as sufficient for acceptance, ignoring that the standard IRR decision rule specifically compares IRR to the firm's MARR (9% < 12%), not to zero.
governing_concept: The IRR decision rule accepts a project only when IRR is greater than or equal to the firm's MARR; a positive IRR that is still below MARR is insufficient for acceptance.
corrective_rule: Always compare IRR to the firm's stated MARR, never to zero or to a generic 'positive' threshold, when applying the IRR accept/reject rule.
exam_trap: A test-taker may reflexively equate 'positive return' with 'acceptable investment,' forgetting that the actual decision rule requires clearing the specific MARR hurdle, not merely exceeding zero.

option_text: NPV ~= USD -27,447; reject
why_wrong: Reverses the NPV subtraction order (Initial Investment − PV of inflows instead of PV of inflows − Initial Investment), which preserves the correct $27,447 magnitude but flips the sign, and consequently flips the accept/reject conclusion to reject.
governing_concept: NPV = −Initial Investment + PV of future cash inflows (i.e., PV of inflows − Initial Investment); the project is accepted when this difference is positive.
corrective_rule: Always compute PV of inflows minus the initial investment, never the reverse, when applying the NPV formula.
exam_trap: A test-taker who correctly discounts the five annual inflows may still subtract in the wrong order when combining with the investment, landing on the right magnitude but the wrong sign and the wrong (reject) conclusion.
calculation_path_if_applicable: Reversed subtraction: Initial Investment − PV of inflows = $200,000 − $227,447 = −$27,447 (verified: 60,000x3.79079=227,447.4; 200,000−227,447.4=−27,447.4).
source_support: CCP practice pool (verified) — NPV calculation and decision; S&K6 Ch.28 Practical Corporate Investment Decision-Making Guide

option_text: NPV ~= USD 100,000; accept
why_wrong: Nets the nominal (undiscounted) total inflows against the investment, ignoring the required 10% discounting of the five annual $60,000 receipts entirely.
governing_concept: NPV requires discounting each future cash flow to present value at the stated rate before netting against the initial investment; nominal cash flow totals cannot be substituted for discounted present values.
corrective_rule: Always discount future cash flows to present value using the stated rate and period count before computing NPV; never net raw, undiscounted cash flow totals against the investment.
exam_trap: A test-taker who forgets to apply the (P/A,10%,5) annuity factor may simply multiply $60,000 x 5 years and subtract the investment, producing a larger, 'no discounting needed' NPV.
source_support: CCP practice pool (verified) — NPV calculation and decision; S&K6 Ch.28 Practical Corporate Investment Decision-Making Guide

option_text: NPV ~= USD 0; indifferent
why_wrong: An NPV of exactly $0 does not correspond to any single clean, reproducible operation on the item's given $200,000 investment, $60,000 annual inflow, 5-year period, or 10% rate; it functions as a plausible 'safe middle' distractor rather than a value reachable by one identifiable arithmetic slip.
governing_concept: NPV = PV of future cash inflows discounted at the stated rate, minus the initial investment; here it computes to approximately $27,447, not $0.
corrective_rule: Always perform the full discounting calculation (P/A factor x annual inflow, minus investment) rather than assuming an 'indifferent/breakeven' result without computing it.
exam_trap: A test-taker unsure of their arithmetic may hedge toward an 'indifferent, NPV≈0' answer as a safe-sounding middle ground rather than trusting a computed positive result.
source_support: CCP practice pool (verified) — NPV calculation and decision; S&K6 Ch.28 Practical Corporate Investment Decision-Making Guide
notes: No clean single-operation origin identified for exactly $0; treated as GENERAL_WRONG_REASON_VERIFIED rather than asserting an unverified specific mechanism.

option_identity: NPV equals zero regardless of MARR
option_text: NPV equals zero regardless of MARR
why_wrong: Fabricates a rule that NPV always equals zero regardless of MARR; NPV is instead a computed value that varies with the discount rate used, and the actual decision rule is to accept when NPV is positive at the firm's MARR.
governing_concept: Under the NPV decision rule, a single independent project should be accepted when NPV is positive when cash flows are discounted at the firm's MARR.
corrective_rule: Compute NPV by actually discounting the project's cash flows at the firm's MARR; do not assume NPV is a fixed value (such as zero) independent of the discount rate.
exam_trap: A test-taker may confuse NPV's decision threshold (compare to zero) with a claim that NPV itself always equals zero, conflating the comparison benchmark with the computed value.

option_identity: NPV is negative at the firm's minimum attractive rate of return (MARR)
option_text: NPV is negative at the firm's minimum attractive rate of return (MARR)
why_wrong: States the acceptance condition backwards; the actual NPV decision rule accepts a project when NPV is POSITIVE at the firm's MARR, not when it is negative.

option_identity: NPV is calculated using the project's own IRR as the discount rate
option_text: NPV is calculated using the project's own IRR as the discount rate
why_wrong: Substitutes the project's own IRR for the firm's MARR as the discount rate; using a project's own IRR to discount its own cash flows always mathematically forces NPV to zero and provides no basis for an accept/reject decision under the NPV rule.
governing_concept: Under the NPV decision rule, a single independent project should be accepted when NPV is positive when cash flows are discounted at the firm's MARR, not at the project's own IRR.
corrective_rule: Always discount cash flows at the firm's MARR (the required return) when applying the NPV decision rule, never at the project's own computed IRR.
exam_trap: A test-taker who knows IRR and NPV are related may mistakenly believe using IRR as the discount rate is a valid or even 'more accurate' way to compute a decision-useful NPV.

corrective_rule: After computing both ROCE values correctly, always select the company with the numerically HIGHER percentage as the better performer.

calculation_path_if_applicable: ROCE(X) = 60/500 = 12%; ROCE(Y) = 60/750 = 8% (both verified correct: 60/500=0.12; 60/750=0.08), but the winner label is swapped: Y (8.0%) is called better than X (12.0%).
source_support: Ch.28, Base Case Economic Indicators (comparative)

option_identity: Both companies have identical ROCE since profit is the same
option_text: Both companies have identical ROCE since profit is the same
why_wrong: Assumes both companies must have identical ROCE simply because they earn the same $60 million profit, ignoring that their asset bases ($500M vs. $750M) differ, which necessarily makes the two ratios different (12.0% vs. 8.0%).
governing_concept: ROCE = Operating Income / Assets Employed; equal numerators (profit) do NOT produce equal ratios when the denominators (assets employed) differ.
corrective_rule: Always divide each company's own profit by its own assets employed; never assume equal profit implies equal ROCE without checking the denominator.
exam_trap: A test-taker who fixates on the identical $60 million profit figure may conclude the companies are 'the same' without dividing in each company's own asset-employed figure.
calculation_path_if_applicable: Falsely assumes ROCE(X) = ROCE(Y) based on equal profit alone, without dividing by each company's own $500M/$750M asset base (correct values are 12.0% and 8.0%, not equal).
source_support: Ch.28, Base Case Economic Indicators (comparative)

option_text: Company X: 8.0% vs. Company Y: 12.0%
why_wrong: Swaps the two companies' computed ROCE values (assigning Y's 8.0% to X and X's 12.0% to Y), transposing the figures between the two parallel scenario branches even though X is actually the higher-ROCE company.
governing_concept: ROCE = Operating Income / Assets Employed, computed independently for each company; each company's own percentage must stay attached to that company.
corrective_rule: After computing each company's ROCE separately, double-check that each percentage is reported next to the correct company label before finalizing the answer.
exam_trap: A test-taker doing both calculations quickly may transpose the two percentage figures when writing up the final comparison, especially if working from memory rather than rechecking each label.
calculation_path_if_applicable: Correct values are ROCE(X)=60/500=12.0%, ROCE(Y)=60/750=8.0%; this option swaps them to X=8.0%, Y=12.0%, an entity/value cross-contamination.
source_support: Ch.28, Base Case Economic Indicators (comparative)

option_text: New tax=$8.80/unit; profit reduced by $8.00/unit
why_wrong: Correctly computes the new tax ($8.80/unit) but then restates the OLD tax figure ($8.00) unchanged as the profit reduction, instead of computing the actual delta between the new and old tax ($8.80 − $8.00 = $0.80).
governing_concept: Profit Reduction = New Tax − Old Tax; the reduction is the CHANGE in the tax component, not either tax figure standing alone.
corrective_rule: Always subtract the old value from the new value to find the change/reduction amount; never report one of the two input figures unchanged as if it were the delta.
exam_trap: A test-taker who correctly computes the new tax may then grab the already-given $8.00 old-tax figure as a 'safe' second answer, rather than computing the actual difference between the two tax figures.
calculation_path_if_applicable: New Tax = $8.00 x 1.10 = $8.80 (correct). Profit reduction restated as old tax figure: $8.00 (not the actual delta of $0.80).
source_support: Ch.28, Revenue—Commercial Issues

option_text: New tax=$8.00/unit (unchanged); no profit impact
why_wrong: Ignores the stated 10% tax increase entirely, treating the tax component as unchanged and concluding there is no profit impact, when the problem explicitly states taxes increase by 10%.
governing_concept: New Tax = Old Tax x 1.10; a stated percentage rate change must be applied to the base figure, not disregarded.
corrective_rule: Always apply a stated percentage rate change to the relevant base figure; never treat an explicitly stated change as having no effect.
exam_trap: A test-taker who is unsure how to apply a percentage increase to an embedded cost component may default to 'no change' rather than working through the multiplication.
source_support: Ch.28, Revenue—Commercial Issues

option_text: New tax=$9.50/unit; profit reduced by $1.50/unit
why_wrong: $9.50/unit new tax and $1.50/unit profit reduction do not correspond to any single clean, reproducible application of a 10% increase to the given $8.00 tax component ($8.00 x 1.10 = $8.80, not $9.50); the precise arithmetic origin of this specific pair of figures cannot be confidently pinned down from the given inputs.
governing_concept: New Tax = Old Tax x 1.10 = $8.00 x 1.10 = $8.80; Profit Reduction = New Tax − Old Tax = $0.80.
corrective_rule: Apply the 10% increase specifically to the given $8.00 tax component, not to the $95.50 selling price or any other figure in the problem.
exam_trap: A test-taker who is unsure which figure the 10% increase applies to may apply it to the wrong base (e.g., the selling price) and arrive at a similarly-sized but incorrect pair of figures.
source_support: Ch.28, Revenue—Commercial Issues
notes: Could not derive a single clean, independently reproducible calculation path for this exact pair of values; treated as GENERAL_WRONG_REASON_VERIFIED rather than asserting an unverified specific mechanism.

option_text: PI=0.80; no, since PI<1.0
why_wrong: Inverts the PI ratio (Initial Investment / PV of future cash flows instead of PV of future cash flows / Initial Investment), producing the mathematical reciprocal of the correct PI and the wrong fund/no-fund conclusion.
governing_concept: Profitability Index (PI) = PV of future cash flows / Initial Investment; a PI greater than 1 means the project should be funded.
corrective_rule: Always place the PV of future cash flows in the numerator and the initial investment in the denominator; never divide the smaller base figure by the larger benefit figure.
exam_trap: A test-taker unsure which figure goes on top may divide investment by cash flows instead of the reverse, and since 0.80 is a 'clean-looking' number below 1, it can look like a legitimate reject signal.
calculation_path_if_applicable: Inverted ratio: Initial Investment / PV of future cash flows = $10,000,000 / $12,500,000 = 0.80 (verified: 10,000,000/12,500,000=0.80).
source_support: Ch.28, Base Case Economic Indicators (Profitability Index)

option_text: PI=1.25; no, since PI exceeds 1.0
why_wrong: Computes the correct PI value (1.25) but then inverts the accept/reject rule, treating PI exceeding 1.0 as a reason NOT to fund the project, when a PI greater than 1.0 is exactly the condition that signals the project should be funded.
governing_concept: A Profitability Index greater than 1.0 means the project creates positive value per unit of investment and should be funded; the correct PI value alone is not enough if the accept/reject rule is then applied backwards.
corrective_rule: After computing PI correctly, apply the rule that PI > 1.0 means fund (accept), not reject; never treat exceeding the 1.0 threshold as a disqualifying result.
exam_trap: A test-taker who correctly computes PI=1.25 may still second-guess the accept/reject direction and pick the option that pairs the right number with the wrong (reversed) conclusion.
source_support: Ch.28, Base Case Economic Indicators (Profitability Index)

why_wrong: Subtracts the initial investment from the PV of future cash flows ($12,500,000 − $10,000,000 = $2,500,000), which computes Net Present Value, not the Profitability Index; PI requires division, not subtraction.
governing_concept: Profitability Index (a ratio, PV/Investment) and Net Present Value (a dollar difference, PV−Investment) are two distinct economic indicators built from the same two inputs by two different operations.
corrective_rule: Use division (PV / Investment) to compute PI; use subtraction (PV − Investment) to compute NPV; never substitute one operation for the other.
exam_trap: A test-taker who is more comfortable with NPV's subtraction than PI's division may default to subtracting the two figures even when the question specifically asks for PI.
source_support: Ch.28, Base Case Economic Indicators (Profitability Index)

why_wrong: $45.00/unit restates the given $45,000,000 total capex figure's leading digits directly as the answer, skipping the required division by the 900,000-unit annual design capacity.
governing_concept: Capex/Unit = Total Capex / Annual Design Capacity (units); the answer must be the computed quotient, not the capex figure restated at a different scale.
corrective_rule: Always divide total capex by the annual design capacity in units; never restate the capex figure's digits directly as the per-unit answer.
exam_trap: A test-taker in a hurry may see '$45' embedded in '$45,000,000' and treat it as a plausible per-unit answer without actually performing the division by 900,000.
calculation_path_if_applicable: Capex figure's leading digits restated unchanged: $45.00 (no division performed).
source_support: Ch.28, Base Case Economic Indicators (Unit Measures)

why_wrong: Results from misreading the $45,000,000 total capex figure's place value as $45,000 (dropping three zeros) before dividing by the 900,000-unit design capacity, producing a per-unit figure that is 1,000 times too small.
governing_concept: Capex/Unit = Total Capex / Annual Design Capacity (units); the full, correctly-scaled capex figure ($45,000,000) must be used in the division.
corrective_rule: Carry the full place value of the given dollar figure through the calculation; double-check zero counts before dividing large dollar amounts.
exam_trap: A test-taker transcribing a large dollar figure by hand may drop zeros, especially when the divisor (900,000) also has several trailing zeros, making a scale mismatch easy to miss.
calculation_path_if_applicable: Misread capex as $45,000: $45,000 / 900,000 x 1,000 scale error ≈ ... equivalently 900,000 / 45,000 = 20 (verified: 900,000/45,000=20), matching this distractor's $20.00/unit.
source_support: Ch.28, Base Case Economic Indicators (Unit Measures)

why_wrong: $900.00/unit restates the given 900,000-unit annual design capacity's leading digits directly as the dollar answer, skipping the required division of total capex by that capacity figure.
governing_concept: Capex/Unit = Total Capex / Annual Design Capacity (units); the answer must be the computed quotient, not the capacity figure restated as a dollar amount.
corrective_rule: Always divide total capex by the annual design capacity in units; never restate the capacity figure's digits directly as a dollar per-unit answer.
exam_trap: A test-taker who confuses which of the two given numbers is the numerator may latch onto the capacity figure (900,000) and present its leading digits as if it were itself the answer.
calculation_path_if_applicable: Capacity figure's leading digits restated unchanged as a dollar amount: $900.00 (no division performed).
source_support: Ch.28, Base Case Economic Indicators (Unit Measures)

option_identity: Rank the alternatives by lowest forecast cost even though revenue and timing effects differ.
option_text: Rank the alternatives by lowest forecast cost even though revenue and timing effects differ.
why_wrong: Ranking alternatives by lowest forecast cost alone ignores that revenue and timing effects differ between them; a defensible profitability analysis must evaluate revenue, cost, and applicable return/margin measures together, not cost in isolation.
governing_concept: Blueprint responsibility 4.L requires evaluating profitability using consistent forecast revenue, cost, and applicable return or margin measures before recommending an alternative, not a single narrow criterion.
corrective_rule: Always evaluate revenue, cost, and return/margin measures together on a consistent forecast basis; never substitute a single-factor criterion (e.g., lowest cost) for the full profitability comparison.
exam_trap: A test-taker may be drawn to the seemingly disciplined-sounding 'lowest cost' criterion, missing that the scenario explicitly says revenue and timing effects differ and must be accounted for too.
source_support: Current CCP Candidate Handbook (May 2026 Blueprint) 4.L; S&K6 Ch.28; Ch.27

option_identity: Use historical sunk cost as the principal basis for selecting the most profitable future alternative.
option_text: Use historical sunk cost as the principal basis for selecting the most profitable future alternative.
why_wrong: Using historical sunk cost as the principal basis for a forward-looking profitability decision lets an already-spent, unrecoverable cost improperly influence the selection of the most profitable future alternative, instead of using consistent forecast revenue/cost/return measures.
governing_concept: Blueprint responsibility 4.L requires evaluating profitability using consistent FORECAST revenue, cost, and applicable return or margin measures, not historical sunk cost.
corrective_rule: Base forward-looking profitability decisions on forecast (future) revenue, cost, and return measures; exclude sunk costs, which cannot be recovered regardless of which alternative is chosen.
exam_trap: A test-taker may feel that money already spent must be 'accounted for' in the decision, falling into the classic sunk-cost fallacy rather than focusing purely on forward-looking figures.
source_support: Current CCP Candidate Handbook (May 2026 Blueprint) 4.L; S&K6 Ch.28; Ch.27

option_identity: Treat a positive projected cash balance as sufficient evidence of superior profitability.
option_text: Treat a positive projected cash balance as sufficient evidence of superior profitability.
why_wrong: A positive projected cash balance reflects liquidity, not profitability; treating it as sufficient evidence of superior profitability skips the required evaluation of consistent forecast revenue, cost, and applicable return or margin measures.
governing_concept: Blueprint responsibility 4.L requires evaluating profitability using consistent forecast revenue, cost, and applicable return or margin measures, not a cash-balance proxy.
corrective_rule: Do not treat a positive cash position as proof of superior profitability; profitability requires its own revenue/cost/return-based evaluation.
exam_trap: A test-taker may equate 'has more cash on hand' with 'is more profitable,' repeating the same profit-versus-liquidity conflation the chapter warns against elsewhere.
source_support: Current CCP Candidate Handbook (May 2026 Blueprint) 4.L; S&K6 Ch.28; Ch.27

option_text: It must be greater than 13%
why_wrong: The solution states 13% is 'generally accepted' as a typical discount rate that varies by industry sector, not a rigid rule that the discount rate 'must be greater than 13%'; the actual defining requirement is that it satisfy investors' required rate of return, whatever that rate is.
governing_concept: The discount rate must satisfy the rate of return required by company investors; a commonly cited figure like 13% is only a general industry reference point, not a fixed minimum threshold.
corrective_rule: Define the discount rate by its function (satisfying investors' required return), not by hard-coding a specific numeric threshold like '13%' as a mandatory minimum.
exam_trap: A test-taker who recalls '13%' as a commonly cited figure from the source may over-literalize it into an absolute 'must exceed 13%' rule rather than understanding it as a variable, investor-driven rate.

option_identity: It is the value of the financing percentage to get a loan
option_text: It is the value of the financing percentage to get a loan
why_wrong: The discount rate is the rate that must be earned to satisfy investors' required rate of return, not the financing percentage needed to obtain a loan; these are two distinct financial concepts (equity/investor return vs. debt financing cost).
governing_concept: The discount rate must satisfy the rate of return required by company investors, who are funding the project expecting a return on their investment.
corrective_rule: Distinguish the discount rate (investor-required return) from a loan's financing percentage (a cost-of-debt concept); do not conflate the two.
exam_trap: A test-taker may associate 'rate' language generically with borrowing/loan interest rates, since both involve percentages tied to financing a project.

option_text: None of the above is correct

governing_concept: The discount rate must satisfy the rate of return required by company investors — a specific, source-supported definition exists among the listed options.
corrective_rule: Before selecting a 'none of the above' option, verify that none of the other listed options actually matches the source; here, one clearly does.
